The request that starts a run of appended changes records the instructions it was sent as an [`InstructionBaselinePart`][pydantic_ai.messages.InstructionBaselinePart]: every block, in order, with the appending ones in full and the others as an [`InstructionDigest`][pydantic_ai.messages.InstructionDigest] (id and content hash), so a long block rewritten on every request isn't stored again each time. Later requests are sent the same prefix and append their changes after it. When the prefix has to change anyway, because a block that isn't appending changed, a block's policy changed, the history was compacted, or a request was sent without instructions (for example because a hook unset them), the request records a new baseline with current values, which costs no more cache than the change itself. The baseline is never sent to a model.

Persist the complete [message history](message-history.md), including these baseline parts, to retain the original prefix when another agent instance continues the conversation. Every previously sent replacement stays in history even after it is superseded. Compaction, or removing the baseline from history, starts a fresh baseline from current instructions. Do not prune old replacements independently if you want to preserve the prefix.

The guarantee concerns instruction-induced prefix changes between baseline resets, with other request inputs unchanged. Changes to tools, models, provider caching rules, or cache expiry can still prevent cache reuse. History written by a newer Pydantic AI version with an instruction source this version doesn't know also starts a fresh baseline.

Each block is sent as a `<context id="...">` element, and the last of them is followed once by the sentence "A later `<context>` element with the same id replaces the earlier one and stays in effect until replaced again." Each replacement or withdrawal is sent as a new element with that id. When a replacement differs from the text the model already has by less than its full length, as when one line of a long memory file is edited, it's sent as a `<context_diff id="...">` element holding a unified diff instead. History still records the complete replacement, along with a hash of the text it replaces: if a [history processor](message-history.md#processing-message-history) removed an earlier change, so the model never saw the text a diff would apply to, the model gets the complete replacement. Closing `</context>`, `</context_diff>` and `</system>` tags in a block's text are escaped, so the text can't end its element early. Models that support mid-conversation system messages receive the replacements that way; other models receive them as `<system>`-tagged user text. History stores only the content, so the prefix is the same on every request and for every model in a [`FallbackModel`][pydantic_ai.models.fallback.FallbackModel].

Whether a model accepts and follows an update is model-dependent: preserving the prefix doesn't suppress provider refusals. See the provider pages for known issues, such as [refusals on repeated prompts](models/anthropic.md#refusals-on-repeated-prompts) on Anthropic.

Instructions that Pydantic AI and [Pydantic AI Harness](harness/index.md) compute themselves append their changes by default: the catalog of [on-demand capabilities](capabilities/on-demand.md) that the `load_capability` tool loads (keyed `capability:deferred_capabilities`), and the Harness [`SubAgents`](harness/subagents.md) listing (`capability:sub_agents`, or the capability's `id`), [`RepoContext`](harness/repo-context.md) context files (`capability:repo_context`, or the capability's `id`), and [`ManagedPrompt`](harness/managed-prompt.md) prompts (`capability:managed-prompt-<name>`, or the capability's `id`). [MCP server instructions](mcp/client.md#server-instructions) that an [`MCPToolset`][pydantic_ai.mcp.MCPToolset] includes do the same (`toolset:<id>`, where a URL toolset's `id` defaults to the server's hostname). A skill added to the workspace, a new sub-agent definition, an edited `AGENTS.md`, a new version of a managed prompt or a server's new instructions between runs of a conversation then extends the cached prompt rather than rewriting it. Instructions you write keep the `'rewrite'` default until you opt in.

!!! note "Scope and trust"
    Append delivery supports always-on agent, capability, and toolset instruction sources. A loaded [on-demand capability](capabilities/on-demand.md)'s instructions are stated in history, in the system voice, after the `load_capability` tool result rather than in the prefix, and their changes are always appended, whatever their `on_change` policy. Realtime sessions warn when given this opt-in and retain their existing delivery behavior; the framework's own appending blocks fall back to rewriting there without a warning. Legacy `system_prompt(dynamic=True)` is unchanged.

    [UI adapters](ui/overview.md) keep instruction baselines and changes in trusted server-side history. Client-submitted instruction delta and baseline parts are stripped with system prompts. Browser-only history therefore starts a new baseline; matching an old value to current text does not authenticate its origin.

    Append delivery does not make instruction callbacks durable. In [durable execution](durable_execution/overview.md), callbacks must be deterministic or obtain changing external values through a [durable capability operation](capabilities/custom.md#durable-capability-operations) or the engine's durable units. Registering a bound async capability method decorated with `@durable_operation` through `capability.instructions(name='state', on_change='append')(capability.read_state)` records its result before history changes are computed. Replay then uses recorded values rather than fresh external reads.

#### Keep untrusted text out of instructions {#untrusted-instruction-text}

Instructions carry operator authority, and appended changes are sent as system messages on models that support them, so the model treats their text as your instruction. Build instructions only from state you control: fixed strings, counts, values from a fixed set, or routing your application resolved. Never put tool arguments, tool output, user input, or retrieved content in them, even in append mode, where escaping closing tags only stops the text from breaking out of its element, not from being obeyed. Send untrusted values to the model in user messages or tool results instead.

## Reflection and self-correction

Validation errors from both function tool parameter validation and [structured output validation](output.md#structured-output) can be passed back to the model with a request to retry.

You can also raise [`ModelRetry`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRetry] from within a [tool](tools.md) or [output function](output.md#output-functions) to tell the model it should retry generating a response.

This is one of [several layers that can retry](retries.md) during a run, each with its own budget.

- The default retry count is **1** but can be altered for the [entire agent][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.__init__] with `retries` or [`AgentRetries`][pydantic_ai.agent.AgentRetries], a [specific tool][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.tool], or [outputs][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.__init__]. Both the tool and output sides of the agent retry budget can also be overridden per run via `agent.run(retries={'tools': ..., 'output': ...})` and friends (or for a block of runs via [`agent.override()`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.override]). At these call sites a bare `int` overrides both budgets, just like at construction — pass a dict such as `retries={'tools': ...}` to override just one. The tool-retry default and its per-run override apply to function tools, output tools, and MCP tools.
- You can access the current retry count from within a tool, output validator, or output function via [`ctx.retry`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.retry].

### How output retries are enforced

Pydantic AI enforces the output retry budget differently depending on how the model returns its final output:

- **Text output path** (`output_type=str`, text-only outputs, empty or unusable model responses): a single global budget is shared across the whole run. Each invalid response consumes one unit of the budget; when it's exhausted, the run raises [`UnexpectedModelBehavior`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UnexpectedModelBehavior] with message `'Exceeded maximum output retries (N)'`.
- **Tool output path** ([`output_type=ToolOutput(...)`](output.md#tool-output), structured outputs): the output retry budget is the *default per-tool limit*. See [Tool Output](output.md#tool-output) for per-tool overrides via [`ToolOutput(max_retries=N)`][pydantic_ai.output.ToolOutput.max_retries].

For how the budget appears inside [output validators](output.md#output-validator-functions) — including what `ctx.max_retries` and `ctx.retry` reflect on each path — see the [Output validators](output.md#output-validator-functions) section.

Tool retries are tracked per tool — see [Tool Execution, Retries, and Failures](tools-advanced.md#tool-retries) for the per-tool counter model and the three configuration levels.

Here's an example:

```python {title="tool_retry.py"}
from pydantic import BaseModel

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext, ModelRetry

from fake_database import DatabaseConn


class ChatResult(BaseModel):
    user_id: int
    message: str


agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    deps_type=DatabaseConn,
    output_type=ChatResult,
)


@agent.tool(retries=2)
def get_user_by_name(ctx: RunContext[DatabaseConn], name: str) -> int:
    """Get a user's ID from their full name."""
    print(name)
    #> John
    #> John Doe
    user_id = ctx.deps.users.get(name=name)
    if user_id is None:
        raise ModelRetry(
            f'No user found with name {name!r}, remember to provide their full name'
        )
    return user_id


result = agent.run_sync(
    'Send a message to John Doe asking for coffee next week', deps=DatabaseConn()
)
print(result.output)
"""
user_id=123 message='Hello John, would you be free for coffee sometime next week? Let me know what works for you!'
"""
```

## Debugging and Monitoring

Agents require a different approach to observability than traditional software. With traditional web endpoints or data pipelines, you can largely predict behavior by reading the code. With agents, this is much harder. The model's decisions are stochastic, and that stochasticity compounds through the agentic loop as the agent reasons, calls tools, observes results, and reasons again. You need to actually see what happened.

This means setting up your application to record what's happening in a way you can review afterward, both during development (to understand and iterate) and in production (to debug issues and monitor behavior). The ergonomics matter too: a plaintext dump of everything that happened isn't a practical way to review agent behavior, even during development. You want tooling that lets you step through each decision and tool call interactively.

We recommend [Pydantic Logfire](https://logfire.pydantic.dev/docs/), which has been designed with Pydantic AI workflows in mind.

### Tracing with Logfire

```python
import logfire

logfire.configure()
logfire.instrument_pydantic_ai()
```

With Logfire instrumentation enabled, every agent run creates a detailed trace showing:

- **Messages exchanged** with the model (system, user, assistant)
- **Tool calls** including arguments and return values
- **Token usage** per request and cumulative
- **Latency** for each operation
- **Errors** with full context

This visibility is invaluable for:

- Understanding why an agent made a specific decision
- Debugging unexpected behavior
- Optimizing performance and costs
- Monitoring production deployments

### Systematic Testing with Evals

For systematic evaluation of agent behavior beyond runtime debugging, [Pydantic Evals](evals.md) provides a code-first framework for testing AI systems:

```python {test="skip" lint="skip" format="skip"}
from pydantic_evals import Case, Dataset

dataset = Dataset(
    name='agent_eval',
    cases=[
        Case(name='capital_question', inputs='What is the capital of France?', expected_output='Paris'),
    ]
)
report = dataset.evaluate_sync(my_agent_function)
```

Evals let you define test cases, run them against your agent, and score the results. When combined with Logfire, evaluation results appear in the web UI for visualization and comparison across runs. See the [Logfire integration guide](evals/how-to/logfire-integration.md) for setup.

### Using Other Backends

Pydantic AI's instrumentation is built on [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/), so you can send traces to any compatible backend. Even if you use the Logfire SDK for its convenience, you can configure it to send data to other backends. See [alternative backends](logfire.md#using-opentelemetry) for setup instructions.

[Full Logfire integration guide →](logfire.md)

## Model errors

If models behave unexpectedly (e.g., the retry limit is exceeded, or their API returns `503`), agent runs will raise [`UnexpectedModelBehavior`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UnexpectedModelBehavior].

In these cases, [`capture_run_messages`][pydantic_ai.capture_run_messages] can be used to access the messages exchanged during the run to help diagnose the issue.

For a run that was cancelled rather than failed, [`RunCancelled`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.RunCancelled] and [`RunCancelled.from_cancellation()`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.RunCancelled.from_cancellation] carry the run's history directly -- see [Cancelling a Run](#cancelling-a-run).

```python {title="agent_model_errors.py"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRetry, UnexpectedModelBehavior, capture_run_messages

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}')


@agent.tool_plain
def calc_volume(size: int) -> int:  # (1)!
    if size == 42:
        return size**3
    else:
        raise ModelRetry('Please try again.')


with capture_run_messages() as messages:  # (2)!
    try:
        result = agent.run_sync('Please get me the volume of a box with size 6.')
    except UnexpectedModelBehavior as e:
        print('An error occurred:', e)
        """
        An error occurred:
        Tool 'calc_volume' exceeded max retries count of 1. Consider raising the retry limit, or see the docs on tool retries: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/tools-toolsets/tools-advanced/#tool-retries
        """
        print('cause:', repr(e.__cause__))
        #> cause: ModelRetry('Please try again.')
        print('messages:', messages)
        """
        messages:
        [
            ModelRequest(
                parts=[
                    UserPromptPart(
                        content='Please get me the volume of a box with size 6.',
                        timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                    )
                ],
                timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                run_id='...',
                conversation_id='...',
            ),
            ModelResponse(
                parts=[
                    ToolCallPart(
                        tool_name='calc_volume',
                        args={'size': 6},
                        tool_call_id='pyd_ai_tool_call_id',
                    )
                ],
                usage=RequestUsage(
                    cost=Decimal('0.000164'), input_tokens=62, output_tokens=4
                ),
                model_name='{{ openai:medium.name }}',
                timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                run_id='...',
                conversation_id='...',
            ),
            ModelRequest(
                parts=[
                    ToolReturnPart(
                        tool_name='calc_volume',
                        content='Please try again.',
                        tool_call_id='pyd_ai_tool_call_id',
                        timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                        outcome='retried',
                        retry=RetryInfo(cause='model_retry', attempt=1, max_retries=1),
                    )
                ],
                timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                run_id='...',
                conversation_id='...',
            ),
            ModelResponse(
                parts=[
                    ToolCallPart(
                        tool_name='calc_volume',
                        args={'size': 6},
                        tool_call_id='pyd_ai_tool_call_id',
                    )
                ],
                usage=RequestUsage(
                    cost=Decimal('0.000216'), input_tokens=68, output_tokens=8
                ),
                model_name='{{ openai:medium.name }}',
                timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                run_id='...',
                conversation_id='...',
            ),
            ModelRequest(
                parts=[],
                timestamp=datetime.datetime(...),
                run_id='...',
                conversation_id='...',
                state='interrupted',
            ),
        ]
        """
    else:
        print(result.output)
```

1. Define a tool that will raise `ModelRetry` repeatedly in this case.
2. [`capture_run_messages`][pydantic_ai.capture_run_messages] is used to capture the messages exchanged during the run.

_(This example is complete, it can be run "as is")_

When a run is cut short by an exception while streaming, an exception inside a tool, or external cancellation, Pydantic AI still captures partial state where it can. Partial [`ModelResponse`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelResponse] and [`ModelRequest`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelRequest] messages have `state='interrupted'` so persistence layers and UIs can distinguish them from complete messages. A response that arrived complete but whose run stopped before acting on it, such as one that crossed a token or cost [usage limit](#usage-limits), is also marked `state='interrupted'`.

For model responses cut short while streaming, interrupted messages contain the response parts streamed before the interruption. For model requests, interrupted messages contain the tool results that completed before tool execution stopped — if none did, the request is still recorded, with no parts, marking the point where the response's tool calls were abandoned. The captured messages reflect exactly what happened — half-finished tool call parts are not turned into synthetic tool results at capture time. When an interrupted history is passed back into a run, it is [repaired automatically](message-history.md#making-histories-provider-valid) before the next model request.

In this example, `get_volume` completes before `get_mass` raises, so the interrupted request contains the completed `get_volume` return:

```python {title="capture_interrupted_run.py"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRequest, capture_run_messages
from pydantic_ai.messages import (
    ModelMessage,
    ModelResponse,
    ToolCallPart,
    ToolReturnPart,
)
from pydantic_ai.models.function import AgentInfo, FunctionModel


def call_tools(_messages: list[ModelMessage], _info: AgentInfo) -> ModelResponse:
    return ModelResponse(
        parts=[
            ToolCallPart(tool_name='get_volume', args={'size': 6}, tool_call_id='volume_call'),
            ToolCallPart(tool_name='get_mass', args={'size': 6}, tool_call_id='mass_call'),
        ]
    )


agent = Agent(FunctionModel(function=call_tools))


@agent.tool_plain(sequential=True)
def get_volume(size: int) -> int:
    return size**3


@agent.tool_plain(sequential=True)
def get_mass(size: int) -> int:
    raise RuntimeError('missing density')


with capture_run_messages() as messages:
    try:
        agent.run_sync('Calculate volume and mass.')
    except RuntimeError as exc:
        print(f'Run failed: {exc}')
        #> Run failed: missing density

interrupted_request = next(
    message for message in messages if isinstance(message, ModelRequest) and message.state == 'interrupted'
)
assert any(
    isinstance(part, ToolReturnPart) and part.tool_name == 'get_volume' and part.content == 216
    for part in interrupted_request.parts
)
```

!!! note
    If you call [`run`][pydantic_ai.agent.AbstractAgent.run], [`run_sync`][pydantic_ai.agent.AbstractAgent.run_sync], or [`run_stream`][pydantic_ai.agent.AbstractAgent.run_stream] more than once within a single `capture_run_messages` context, `messages` will represent the messages exchanged during the first call only.

    `capture_run_messages` contexts can be nested: each context captures the runs for which it is the innermost active context. A run started inside a nested context is captured by that nested context, not by any enclosing one. This means you can wrap a nested agent run (for example inside a tool that calls another agent) in its own `capture_run_messages` to inspect that inner run's messages independently.

## Recovering a failed run's messages {#recovering-a-failed-run}

A run that raises, whether with [`UsageLimitExceeded`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UsageLimitExceeded], [`UnexpectedModelBehavior`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UnexpectedModelBehavior], another [`AgentRunError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.AgentRunError], or an exception from one of your tools, returns no result, but the work it did before the error is still in its messages. The exceptions don't carry those messages, except [`RunCancelled`](#message-history-after-cancellation). To keep them, wrap the run in [`capture_run_messages`][pydantic_ai.capture_run_messages], which records them as the run goes, including the [interrupted](#model-errors) request or response of the step that failed.

To continue from where the run stopped instead of starting over, pass the captured messages as `message_history` and no new prompt. The new run picks up from the last request, so tool calls that already ran, and any side effects they had, aren't repeated:

```python {title="recover_failed_run.py"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, UsageLimitExceeded, UsageLimits, capture_run_messages

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}')


@agent.tool_plain
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    return 'Shipped on 2032-01-02.'


def answer(prompt: str) -> str:
    with capture_run_messages() as messages:
        try:
            result = agent.run_sync(prompt, usage_limits=UsageLimits(request_limit=1))
            return result.output
        except UsageLimitExceeded as e:
            print(e)
            """
            The next request would exceed the request_limit of 1. Consider raising the limit, or see the docs on usage limits for budget-aware patterns: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/agent/#usage-limits
            """
    resumed = agent.run_sync(message_history=messages)  # (1)!
    return resumed.output


print(answer('What is the status of order 1234?'))
#> Order 1234 shipped on 2032-01-02.
```

1. This run starts outside the `capture_run_messages` block, since within one block `messages` holds only the first run's messages. Given the history and no prompt, it continues from the `get_order_status` result the failed run already has.

_(This example is complete, it can be run "as is")_

The resumed run is a new run: its usage, and the [usage limits](#usage-limits) checked against it, start from zero. When a token or cost limit is crossed, the response that crossed it is kept in the captured messages with `state='interrupted'`, so the resumed run doesn't request it again (see [usage limits](#usage-limits)), unless a hook rejected that response with [`ModelRetry`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRetry] ([#11425](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/11425)). To resume later or in another process, [store the messages](message-history.md) and load them back first.

# `pydantic_ai.realtime`

Support for **realtime, bidirectional speech-to-speech models** (OpenAI Realtime, OpenAI GPT-Live,
Azure OpenAI, Gemini Live, xAI Grok Voice, Eleven Realtime, ElevenLabs Agents, and any other provider that
streams audio in and out over a persistent connection).

Unlike [`Model`][pydantic_ai.models.Model], which is request-response, a realtime model opens a
long-lived connection: you stream audio (or text/images) in, and consume audio, transcripts, and
tool calls as they arrive. The high-level entry point is
[`Agent.realtime()`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.realtime], followed by
[`AgentRealtime.session()`][pydantic_ai.agent.AgentRealtime.session], which wires the agent's tools and
instructions into a session and runs the tool loop for you. See the [Realtime guide](../realtime/overview.md)
for a walkthrough.

The flow of a session:

```mermaid
graph LR
    App -- "send(): RealtimeSessionInput" --> S[RealtimeSession]
    S -- "send(): RealtimeInput" --> C[RealtimeConnection]
    M[RealtimeModel] -- "connect()" --> C
    C -- "RealtimeFrame" --> S
    S -- "RealtimeEvent" --> App
```

A [`RealtimeModel`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeModel] opens a
[`RealtimeConnection`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection] (the provider-specific transport).
A [`RealtimeSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession] wraps that connection: it translates the
low-level codec events into the shared message/part event vocabulary from
[`pydantic_ai.messages`][pydantic_ai.messages], builds ordinary
[`ModelMessage`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelMessage] history, and executes tools automatically —
intercepting each [`ToolCall`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolCall], running it, sending the
[`ToolResult`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolResult] back, and emitting a
[`FunctionToolCallEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.FunctionToolCallEvent] then a
[`FunctionToolResultEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.FunctionToolResultEvent]. Every tool runs in the
background, so a slow one never blocks the session; whether the *model* keeps speaking meanwhile is
provider-specific (see [Concurrent tool execution](../realtime/tools.md#concurrent-tool-execution)).

## Overview

**Provider abstractions & session**

| Object | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [`RealtimeModel`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeModel] | Provider ABC; `connect()` opens a connection. |
| [`RealtimeModelSettings`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeModelSettings] | Settings shared by realtime providers. |
| [`TurnDetection`][pydantic_ai.realtime.TurnDetection] | Cross-provider automatic VAD sensitivity, padding, and silence configuration. |
| [`KnownRealtimeModelName`][pydantic_ai.realtime.KnownRealtimeModelName] / [`infer_realtime_model`][pydantic_ai.realtime.infer_realtime_model] | Provider-prefixed model IDs and inference. |
| [`RealtimeConnection`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection] | Provider ABC; `send()` content in, `frames()` of codec and lifecycle events out. |
| [`RealtimeSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession] | Wraps a connection with automatic concurrent tool dispatch. |

**Browser / WebRTC** — for browser voice agents, the media flows browser ↔ provider directly while the
backend runs a control-plane sideband (OpenAI and Azure OpenAI; see [Deployment](../realtime/deployment.md#browser-webrtc-server-sideband)):

| Object | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [`RealtimeModel.answer_webrtc_offer`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeModel.answer_webrtc_offer] | Relay the browser's SDP offer; return the SDP answer and a [`WebRTCAnswer`][pydantic_ai.realtime.WebRTCAnswer] / [`WebRTCSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.WebRTCSession]. |
| [`RealtimeModel.create_client_secret`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeModel.create_client_secret] | Mint an ephemeral [`RealtimeClientSecret`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeClientSecret] for a browser client. |
| [`AgentRealtime.session(provider_session=…)`][pydantic_ai.agent.AgentRealtime.session] | Attach the sideband session to a [`RealtimeProviderSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeProviderSession] (e.g. a [`WebRTCSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.WebRTCSession]) and run the agent. |

**Inputs** — [`RealtimeSession.send`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.send] accepts session content
only, in the shared message vocabulary ([`RealtimeSessionInput`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSessionInput]):
plain `str`, image/audio [`BinaryContent`][pydantic_ai.messages.BinaryContent] (including
[`BinaryImage`][pydantic_ai.messages.BinaryImage] and
[`BinaryAudio`][pydantic_ai.messages.BinaryAudio]), or a sequence of
these. A string solicits a response, while an image is context-only by default; use `respond` to
override either behavior. Turn-taking and interruption go through the dedicated
[`RealtimeSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession] methods (`commit_audio()`, `clear_audio()`,
`create_response()`, `interrupt()`), not `send()`. Use
[`RealtimeSession.enqueue()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.enqueue] to queue text or system
prompt parts for delivery after the active response, or once the model is idle.

**Consumption views** —
[`RealtimeSession.stream_audio()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.stream_audio] yields model
audio chunks ready for playback, while
[`RealtimeSession.stream_transcripts()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.stream_transcripts]
yields finalized speech from both speakers or live deltas with `delta=True`. These bounded views can
run concurrently with each other and with the session's raw event iterator.
[`RealtimeSession.wait_for_reply()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.wait_for_reply] waits
until the model has finished the reply it owes, spanning the whole of a tool-calling turn, and runs
alongside an active event iterator rather than competing with it.
[`RealtimeSession.wait_for_playback()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.wait_for_playback]
waits until the single audio view has accounted for all audio emitted so far, whether it was
played or discarded.
[`RealtimeSession.close()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.close] ends the session and every
live view; [`RealtimeSession.closed`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.closed] exposes its state.
The session starts receiving at whichever comes first: the first outbound call, the first
`stream_audio()` or `stream_transcripts()` view, or the first `async for` over the session. It does
not start on entry, so a view created inside the session block — as every example here does — cannot
miss output the model produced before it subscribed. A fatal receive failure or a tool failure is
raised from active event iteration, which can go on after a tool failure; without an active
iterator, the views end and context exit raises it.
The next outbound session method raises an already-ended receive side's failure first, and the same
failure is never delivered twice.

The low-level [`RealtimeConnection.send`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection.send] accepts the
normalized [`RealtimeInput`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeInput] — a `str` text turn, a
[`TextContext`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.TextContext] item added without soliciting a reply, a raw-PCM
[`BinaryAudio`][pydantic_ai.messages.BinaryAudio] chunk, or a
[`BinaryImage`][pydantic_ai.messages.BinaryImage] frame — which additionally includes the
turn-control verbs ([`CommitAudio`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.CommitAudio],
[`ClearAudio`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ClearAudio],
[`CreateResponse`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.CreateResponse],
[`CancelResponse`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.CancelResponse], and
[`TruncateOutput`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.TruncateOutput]) that those session methods emit, plus
[`ToolResult`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolResult] — which the session sends itself as each tool
completes.

**Connection events** — [`RealtimeCodecEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeCodecEvent], the low-level codec
vocabulary yielded by a connection:
[`AudioDelta`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.AudioDelta],
[`OutputTranscript`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.OutputTranscript],
[`InputTranscript`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.InputTranscript],
[`ToolCall`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolCall],
[`ToolCallCancelled`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolCallCancelled],
[`ResponseDone`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ResponseDone],
[`RealtimeInputSpeechStartEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeInputSpeechStartEvent],
[`RealtimeInputSpeechEndEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeInputSpeechEndEvent],
[`RealtimeOutputSpeechStartEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeOutputSpeechStartEvent],
[`RealtimeOutputSpeechEndEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeOutputSpeechEndEvent],
[`RealtimeInputTranscriptionErrorEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeInputTranscriptionErrorEvent],
[`RealtimeResponseInterruptedEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeResponseInterruptedEvent],
[`RealtimeSessionReconnectEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSessionReconnectEvent],
[`ConversationCreated`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ConversationCreated],
[`ConversationItemCreated`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ConversationItemCreated],
[`InputRejected`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.InputRejected],
[`PartStartEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.PartStartEvent],
[`PartEndEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.PartEndEvent],
[`SessionUsage`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.SessionUsage],
and [`RealtimeSessionErrorEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSessionErrorEvent].

**Lifecycle events** — [`LifecycleEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.LifecycleEvent], which a connection
yields with its codec events, each [`RealtimeFrame`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.RealtimeFrame] from
[`RealtimeConnection.frames()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection.frames] holding what one provider
message made. They say what the codec events can't: where each response starts and ends
([`ResponseStarted`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.ResponseStarted] /
[`ResponseEnded`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.ResponseEnded]) and which inputs it answers (corrected with
[`AnswersRevised`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.AnswersRevised] when the connection learns better), where each
spoken turn starts, joins the conversation, and gets the last of its audio and transcript
([`UserTurnStarted`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.UserTurnStarted] /
[`UserTurnEnded`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.UserTurnEnded] /
[`UserTurnClosed`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.UserTurnClosed]), where each input joins it
([`InputAdded`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InputAdded]), and which inputs no response will answer
([`InputLost`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InputLost] /
[`ResponseRequestRefused`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.ResponseRequestRefused]), and which tool calls' results
it won't answer either ([`ToolCallsAbandoned`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.ToolCallsAbandoned]). The session
builds history, usage, and [`wait_for_reply()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.wait_for_reply] from them.

**Implementing a connection** — subclass [`RealtimeConnection`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection]
and implement [`send()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection.send] and
[`frames()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.RealtimeConnection.frames]. A protocol that identifies its responses,
turns, and inputs (as the OpenAI Realtime API does) is best translated into lifecycle events directly. One that
identifies none of them (as Gemini Live and OpenAI GPT-Live don't) can hand each input it sends and each
provider message it reads to an [`InferredLifecycle`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle], which
works the lifecycle out from their order. Either way, a connection that names the output items its codec events
stream (their `item_id`) can say more about one:
[`OutputItemDetails`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.OutputItemDetails] keeps what the provider says about it on
the part it makes, and [`OutputItemCut`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.OutputItemCut] reports how much of it the
listener heard, which can come after its response ended and revises the copy history recorded. Here, a reply to a
text turn is a response that answers it:

```python
import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Sequence

from pydantic_ai.realtime.codec import (
    OutputTranscript,
    RealtimeCodecEvent,
    RealtimeConnection,
    RealtimeInput,
    ResponseDone,
)
from pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle import InferredLifecycle, LifecycleEvent, RealtimeFrame


class EchoConnection(RealtimeConnection):
    """Says each text turn back: a stand-in for a protocol that identifies nothing."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lifecycle = InferredLifecycle(transcribes=False)
        self._said: asyncio.Queue[str] = asyncio.Queue()

    async def send(self, content: RealtimeInput) -> Sequence[LifecycleEvent]:
        # Reports the input, and that it failed if writing it raises.
        with self._lifecycle.sending(content):
            if isinstance(content, str):
                self._said.put_nowait(content)  # (where a real connection writes to its transport)
        # Where it joined the conversation, which the protocol doesn't acknowledge.
        return self._lifecycle.take_pending()

    def frames(self) -> AsyncIterator[RealtimeFrame]:
        return self._lifecycle.frames(self._codec_events())

    async def _codec_events(self) -> AsyncIterator[RealtimeCodecEvent]:
        while True:  # (where a real connection reads its transport)
            text = await self._said.get()
            yield OutputTranscript(text=text, is_final=True)
            yield ResponseDone()


async def main():
    connection = EchoConnection()
    print(await connection.send('Hello!'))
    #> [InputAdded(input_id=0)]
    frames = connection.frames()
    for _ in range(2):
        print([type(event).__name__ for event in await anext(frames)])
        #> ['ResponseStarted', 'OutputTranscript']
        #> ['ResponseDone', 'ResponseEnded']
```

`frames()` ends once the connection is gone: an `InferredLifecycle` ends what was under way on it then, as
[`connection_lost()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.connection_lost] does for a connection
that re-dials. A connection that reads each provider message itself passes its codec events to
[`frame_for()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.frame_for] to get the frame to yield.

The inference assumes what most providers do: the user's words can be transcribed after the model started
answering them, output audio is the model speaking, and audio the model answers before any transcript of it came
is a spoken turn. A provider that departs from that gets a subclass overriding `InferredLifecycle`'s extension
points: [`transcripts_lag_replies`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.transcripts_lag_replies],
[`audio_starts_response`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.audio_starts_response],
[`untranscribed_audio_is_a_turn`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.untranscribed_audio_is_a_turn],
[`inputs_cut_off_replies`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.inputs_cut_off_replies],
and [`takes_turn()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.takes_turn].

Which inputs a response answers settles each input's reply obligation, which is what
[`wait_for_reply()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession.wait_for_reply] and
[`RealtimeTurnCompleteEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeTurnCompleteEvent] wait for, so only the response that
answers an input may name it. A connection that can't tell yet names its best guess in `ResponseStarted.answers`
(with `basis='inferred'`) and corrects it with an
[`AnswersRevised`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.AnswersRevised] once it can: `released` hands inputs the response
turned out not to answer to a later one, as `InferredLifecycle` does for a response an input cut off (with
`inputs_cut_off_replies`, telling it when the provider heard the user speak with
[`speech_heard()`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.InferredLifecycle.speech_heard], where no
`RealtimeInputSpeechStartEvent` says so), and `claimed`
settles inputs sent while a response was under way that it answers after all, as GPT-Live does by speaking to text
in the reply it is giving. Neither moves anything in history.

A provider can also give up on tool calls before their results are in: Eleven Realtime does once it starts a reply to
the user, and GPT-Live when its delegated backend fails. The connection then names them in a
[`ToolCallsAbandoned`][pydantic_ai.realtime.lifecycle.ToolCallsAbandoned]: the tools keep running and their results
are recorded, but no reply to them is waited for, so the exchange ends with the reply that is under way. Unlike a
[`ToolCallCancelled`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolCallCancelled], it doesn't stop them.

**Session events** — [`RealtimeEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeEvent], yielded by a
session. The session translates codec events into the shared vocabulary from
[`pydantic_ai.messages`][pydantic_ai.messages]: content streams as
[`PartStartEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.PartStartEvent] /
[`PartDeltaEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.PartDeltaEvent] /
[`PartEndEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.PartEndEvent] (carrying shared message parts including
[`SpeechPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.SpeechPart], [`TextPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.TextPart],
[`ToolCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolCallPart], and
[`NativeToolReturnPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolReturnPart]), tool execution as
[`FunctionToolCallEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.FunctionToolCallEvent] /
[`FunctionToolResultEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.FunctionToolResultEvent], deferred calls and their inline resolution as
[`DeferredToolRequestsEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.DeferredToolRequestsEvent] /
[`DeferredToolResultsEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.DeferredToolResultsEvent], enqueued-message delivery as
[`EnqueuedMessagesEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.EnqueuedMessagesEvent], events emitted with
[`RunContext.emit`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.emit] as the
[`CustomEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.CustomEvent] or [`CapabilityEvent`][pydantic_ai.messages.CapabilityEvent]
that was emitted, and the rest as the control-plane events above (`RealtimeInputSpeechStartEvent`, `RealtimeInputSpeechEndEvent`,
`RealtimeOutputSpeechStartEvent`, `RealtimeOutputSpeechEndEvent`, `RealtimeInputTranscriptionErrorEvent`,
`RealtimeResponseInterruptedEvent`, `RealtimeSessionReconnectEvent`, and `RealtimeSessionErrorEvent`), plus
[`RealtimeTurnCompleteEvent`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeTurnCompleteEvent], which the
session synthesizes rather than reading off the wire. Usage updates are accumulated on the session and are not yielded.

The lower-level codec vocabulary is documented in
[`pydantic_ai.realtime.codec`](realtime/codec.md), and each provider in its own module:
[`pydantic_ai.realtime.openai`](realtime/openai.md), [`pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live`](realtime/openai_live.md),
[`pydantic_ai.realtime.google`](realtime/google.md), [`pydantic_ai.realtime.xai`](realtime/xai.md),
[`pydantic_ai.realtime.azure`](realtime/azure.md), [`pydantic_ai.realtime.elevenlabs`](realtime/elevenlabs.md),
and [`pydantic_ai.realtime.elevenlabs_agents`](realtime/elevenlabs_agents.md).

::: pydantic_ai.realtime

# `pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live`

The OpenAI GPT-Live API provider. Requires the `openai-realtime` optional group
(`pip install "pydantic-ai-slim[openai-realtime]"`), which currently requires `openai>=3.31.0`.
`openai` 3.12 added Live's event types.

GPT-Live is a different protocol from the [OpenAI Realtime API](openai.md), not a model served by it,
so [`OpenAILiveModel`][pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live.OpenAILiveModel] shares no event mapping with
[`OpenAIRealtimeModel`][pydantic_ai.realtime.openai.OpenAIRealtimeModel]; the model name is what picks
between them. The Live model runs the spoken conversation and delegates the work to a backend model
configured through
[`OpenAILiveResponsesDelegation`][pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live.OpenAILiveResponsesDelegation] in
[`OpenAILiveModelSettings`][pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live.OpenAILiveModelSettings], which receives the
agent's instructions and tools and calls them as ordinary
[`ToolCall`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ToolCall]s.

Live owns turn-taking entirely, so there is no manual turn control, interruption, or truncation, and
no turn-detection setting. It sends no end-of-response frame either: the connection synthesizes
[`ResponseDone`][pydantic_ai.realtime.codec.ResponseDone] after `openai_live_turn_silence_ms` of
silence, and the profile reports `synthesizes_turn_boundary=True`. Text is delivered as context
rather than as a user turn, seeding is text-only, and usage is reported as billable audio seconds
instead of tokens. Authentication comes from an
[`OpenAIProvider`][pydantic_ai.providers.openai.OpenAIProvider]; Azure OpenAI does not serve Live. See
the [GPT-Live documentation](../../realtime/openai.md#gpt-live-models) for the full story.

::: pydantic_ai.realtime.openai_live

description: "Send agent runs and model requests through provider batch APIs, at about half the price, with Pydantic AI's BatchModelRequests capability and model_request_batch."

# Batch Processing

Anthropic, OpenAI and Google offer batch APIs: you submit many requests as one job, and the provider works through them when it has capacity, at about half the standard price. You get results later rather than straight away: Anthropic and OpenAI give a batch a 24-hour window, and Google targets 24 hours and expires a job after 48. Many batches finish much sooner, but none of these windows is a guarantee, and a request the provider didn't get to in time is [submitted again](#failed-requests).

That trade-off suits work that isn't waiting on a user, such as running [evals](evals.md), classifying or extracting data from many records, and generating data offline. It doesn't suit interactive use, or agents that take many turns: every model request of a run, including each one that follows a tool call, is a separate batch round trip.

Pydantic AI supports batch APIs at three levels:

- The [`BatchModelRequests`](#agents) [capability](capabilities/overview.md) sends an agent's model requests through the batch API, without changing how you run the agent. With [`PendingModelResponse`](#ending-a-run-while-it-waits), a run can end once its request is submitted, and be resumed later to collect the result.
- [`model_request_batch`](#direct-batch-requests) sends a list of model requests as a batch and waits for the responses.
- The [`batch_*` methods on `Model`](#submit-now-collect-later) are the low-level primitives the other two are built on: use them to manage batch jobs yourself, without agents.

## Supported providers and APIs {#supported-models}

| Model | Notes |
|---|---|
| [`AnthropicModel`](models/anthropic.md#batch-api) | The Claude API's Message Batches. Not available on Bedrock, Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry. |
| [`OpenAIResponsesModel`](models/openai.md#batch-api) | OpenAI's Batch API. Not available with `OpenAIChatModel` or Azure OpenAI. On by default with `OpenAIProvider`, including with a custom `base_url`; providers with their own class can [opt in](models/openai.md#batch-api). |
| [`GoogleModel`](models/google.md#batch-api) | The Gemini API's Batch Mode. Not available on Vertex AI. |
| [`TestModel`][pydantic_ai.models.test.TestModel] and [`FunctionModel`][pydantic_ai.models.function.FunctionModel] | Run a batch's requests immediately and in memory, for [testing](testing.md#testing-batch-processing). |

Batching isn't available through [Pydantic AI Gateway](gateway.md) yet: use the provider directly, with its own API key.

These are the APIs Pydantic AI can batch through. Which models a provider serves in batches is up to the provider: see its batch API documentation, linked from each provider's page, which also lists its limits on batch size.

Whether a model has a batch API is a [profile](models/overview.md#models-and-providers) flag: [`anthropic_supports_message_batches`][pydantic_ai.profiles.anthropic.AnthropicModelProfile.anthropic_supports_message_batches], [`openai_supports_batch_api`][pydantic_ai.profiles.openai.OpenAIModelProfile.openai_supports_batch_api] or [`google_supports_batch_api`][pydantic_ai.profiles.google.GoogleModelProfile.google_supports_batch_api]. Pass `profile=` to the model to set it where the default is wrong for your endpoint. Batching a model without a batch API raises a [`UserError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError].

### Cost

Responses from a batch carry `provider_details['processing'] == 'batch'`, so [`ModelResponse.cost()`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelResponse.cost], `usage.cost` and [usage limits](agent.md#usage-limits) use batch prices from [`genai-prices`](https://github.com/pydantic/genai-prices).

## Batching agent runs {#agents}

Add a [`BatchModelRequests`][pydantic_ai.capabilities.BatchModelRequests] capability to an agent and run it as usual. Runs started together, here with `asyncio.gather`, have their requests collected into one batch:

```python {title="batch_agent.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
import asyncio
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import BatchModelRequests


class Triage(BaseModel):
    category: Literal['billing', 'bug', 'account', 'other']
    urgent: bool


agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:medium }}',
    output_type=Triage,
    instructions='Triage this support ticket.',
    capabilities=[BatchModelRequests()],
)

tickets = [
    'I was charged twice for my subscription this month.',
    'The CSV export stops after 1,000 rows.',
    'How do I change the email address on my account?',
]


async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(agent.run(ticket) for ticket in tickets), return_exceptions=True)  # (1)!
    for ticket, result in zip(tickets, results):
        if isinstance(result, BaseException):
            print(f'{ticket!r} failed: {result!r}')
        else:
            print(result.output)
            #> category='billing' urgent=True
            #> category='bug' urgent=False
            #> category='account' urgent=False
```

1. A request that fails only fails its own run, not the others in its batch. With `return_exceptions=True`, you get each run's result or error.

### What happens while a request waits

Each model request is queued until its batch holds `max_requests` requests or its oldest request has waited `max_wait`, and then submitted. The run waits while the batch is processed, checking on it at growing intervals, and continues when the result arrives, as if the request had been answered live. That can take minutes or hours, and so can the `await` above: to end a run once its request is submitted and collect the result later, use [`PendingModelResponse`](#ending-a-run-while-it-waits).

Tools, structured output, output validation and retries work as usual, and each model request in a run goes into whichever batch is being collected when it's made. A run that needs several model requests, for example to call tools or to retry after an output validator raised [`ModelRetry`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRetry], takes several batch round trips, each of which can take as long as the provider's batch window. [Usage limits](agent.md#usage-limits) apply to each run as usual.

Only requests made at about the same time share a batch: runs awaited one after another each wait `max_wait` alone and get a batch each.

### Settings

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 1,000 | The most requests in one batch. The provider's own limit caps it. |
| `max_wait` | 30 seconds | How long the oldest queued request waits for others before its batch is submitted. Later requests never extend it. `None` submits a batch only when it's full or when you call [`flush()`][pydantic_ai.capabilities.BatchModelRequests.flush]. |
| `max_resubmissions` | 2 | How many new batches a request that [failed on the provider's side](#failed-requests) is submitted in before its error is raised. |
| `poll_interval` | 30 seconds | How long a request waits before first checking its batch. The interval grows by half after every check. |
| `max_poll_interval` | 10 minutes | The longest wait between checks. |

A batch is also submitted early when the next request would take it past the provider's size limit. Raise `max_requests` when you make many more requests at a time, to submit fewer, larger batches: providers limit how many batches can be in progress at once.

A run that takes several batch round trips waits up to `max_wait`, plus the time until the next check, for each, on top of the provider's own time. Lower `max_poll_interval` when that adds up, at the cost of more status requests.

### Sharing batches between agents

Each `BatchModelRequests` instance collects its own batches. Add the same instance to several agents, or pass it to runs with `capabilities=`, and their requests share batches:

```python {title="batch_shared.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
import asyncio

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import BatchModelRequests

batching = BatchModelRequests()
replier = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', instructions='Draft a reply to this support ticket.', capabilities=[batching])
summarizer = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', instructions='Summarize this customer feedback in a few words.')


async def main():
    reply, summary = await asyncio.gather(
        replier.run('The app crashes whenever I upload a photo.'),
        summarizer.run(
            'I love the new dashboard, but it takes ages to load on my laptop.',
            capabilities=[batching],  # (1)!
        ),
    )
    print(reply.output)
    #> Sorry about that! We're looking into photo uploads and will update you soon.
    print(summary.output)
    #> Likes the new dashboard, but it loads slowly.
```

1. An agent without the capability can opt individual runs into batching by passing it to `run()`.

### Agent specs {#agent-specs}

`BatchModelRequests` can be declared in an [agent spec](agent-spec.md), with its settings as keyword arguments. Give each duration as a number of seconds or as an ISO 8601 duration, like `PT5M`:

```yaml {title="batch_agent.yaml" test="skip"}
model: {{ anthropic:medium }}
instructions: Triage this support ticket.
capabilities:
  - BatchModelRequests:
      max_requests: 5000
      max_wait: PT5M
```

Each agent built from a spec gets a `BatchModelRequests` instance of its own: its runs share batches with each other, but not with the runs of other agents, even ones built from the same spec. To share batches between agents built from specs, leave the capability out of the specs and pass one instance to their runs with `capabilities=`, as above.

## Submitting now and collecting later {#ending-a-run-while-it-waits}

A batch can take hours, which is longer than many processes should wait. Add [`PendingModelResponse`][pydantic_ai.output.PendingModelResponse] to the agent's `output_type`, and a run ends as soon as its request has been submitted, with a `PendingModelResponse` as its output. The run's message history ends in the pending response, which records the batch, so you can store the history and run the agent again with it later, in this process or another. That run checks on the batch once: if the result has arrived, the run continues as usual, and otherwise it ends with a `PendingModelResponse` again.

```python {title="batch_pending.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel

from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelMessagesTypeAdapter, PendingModelResponse
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import BatchModelRequests


class Triage(BaseModel):
    category: Literal['billing', 'bug', 'account', 'other']
    urgent: bool


agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:medium }}',
    output_type=[Triage, PendingModelResponse],
    instructions='Triage this support ticket.',
    capabilities=[BatchModelRequests(max_wait=timedelta(seconds=5))],  # (1)!
)


async def submit(tickets: list[str]) -> list[bytes]:
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(agent.run(ticket) for ticket in tickets))  # (2)!
    return [result.all_messages_json() for result in results]  # (3)!


async def collect(stored_messages: bytes) -> Triage | bytes:
    result = await agent.run(message_history=ModelMessagesTypeAdapter.validate_json(stored_messages))
    if isinstance(result.output, PendingModelResponse):
        return result.all_messages_json()  # (4)!
    return result.output


async def main():
    stored = await submit(
        [
            'I was charged twice for my subscription this month.',
            'The CSV export stops after 1,000 rows.',
        ]
    )
    # Later, for example from a scheduled job:
    for messages in stored:
        print(await collect(messages))
        #> category='billing' urgent=True
        #> category='bug' urgent=False
```

1. Submitting a request waits up to `max_wait` for more requests to join its batch. A script that starts its runs together and exits can lower it.
2. Start the runs together, so their requests share a batch: runs awaited one after another each wait `max_wait` alone and get a batch each.
3. Store these, for example in a database, and load them wherever you collect the results.
4. The batch is still being processed: store the new history in place of the old one, and check again later.

Collect with `BatchModelRequests` too: resuming the history without it raises a [`UserError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError], rather than sending the waiting request again as a new request at the full price. If the agent's model was chosen dynamically, for example by [`SelectModel`](capabilities/select-model.md), resuming also raises a `UserError` unless you pass the model that submitted the request to the run as `model=`, so store the model's name with the history.

A run that needs several model requests, for example to call tools, ends with a `PendingModelResponse` for each of them. Each run in a submit/collect cycle counts the request in its own [`usage.requests`][pydantic_ai.usage.RunUsage.requests], so adding up `usage.requests` across the runs counts a request once per run, while its tokens and cost are only counted by the run that received the result. This works for any request the provider keeps working on after it's been sent, including [OpenAI background mode](models/openai.md#background-mode).

The process that collects a batch doesn't need the API key that submitted it: the provider decides who may check on a batch, so a rotated key of the same project or workspace works. Checks of one batch within `poll_interval` of each other share one status request, and its results are downloaded once while they're cached, so collecting many stored histories costs about one check per batch rather than one per run. The cache keeps the results of the last 32 batches that ended, up to 256 MB of them, so collect the histories of one batch together rather than interleaved with those of many others.

A batch left for a later run like this keeps running whether or not anything collects it, so collect results well within the provider's [retention window](#retention).

## Durable execution

Without `PendingModelResponse` in the output type, a run waits for its batch, and you only get its message history once it ends. If your process may stop while a batch is processed, end runs with a `PendingModelResponse`, or use [durable execution](durable_execution/overview.md).

With Temporal, DBOS or Prefect, add `BatchModelRequests` to the agent alongside its durability capability. Submitting a request and every check on its batch run as separate durable steps, so a run that's interrupted while its batch is processed, for example by a deployment, continues from the same batch when it's recovered. Under Temporal and DBOS, the waits between checks are durable too. Requests are collected into batches per worker process: the requests of concurrent workflow runs on one worker share batches. Temporal and DBOS don't support capabilities passed to a run inside a workflow, so there the capability has to be on the agent.

```python {title="batch_temporal.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
from pydantic import BaseModel
from temporalio import workflow

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import BatchModelRequests
from pydantic_ai.durable_exec.temporal import PydanticAIWorkflow, TemporalDurability


class Extraction(BaseModel):
    remote: bool
    countries: list[str]


agent = Agent(
    '{{ google:medium }}',
    name='extractor',
    output_type=Extraction,
    instructions='Extract the remote-work details from this job posting.',
    capabilities=[BatchModelRequests(), TemporalDurability()],
)


@workflow.defn
class ExtractPosting(PydanticAIWorkflow):  # (1)!
    __pydantic_ai_agents__ = [agent]

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, posting: str) -> Extraction:
        result = await agent.run(posting)
        return result.output
```

1. Start one workflow per posting: the requests of the workflows running on a worker share batches, and no worker slot is held while a batch is processed. See [Temporal](durable_execution/temporal.md) for running the worker and starting workflows.

With [DBOS](durable_execution/dbos.md) or [Prefect](durable_execution/prefect.md), put [`DBOSDurability`][pydantic_ai.durable_exec.dbos.DBOSDurability] or [`PrefectDurability`][pydantic_ai.durable_exec.prefect.PrefectDurability] next to `BatchModelRequests` instead, and run the agent in a DBOS workflow or a Prefect flow. Under Prefect, the waits between checks are plain sleeps in the flow, which a retried flow run sleeps again.

Once the step that submitted a request has completed, replaying or recovering the workflow reuses its recorded result, so the request isn't submitted again. The one exception is a step that's retried after the provider created its batch but before the step completed, for example because the worker crashed, or because the step timed out: like any model request, the retry sends the request again, which submits it in another batch. A request waits for its batch to be submitted inside its step, so keep `max_wait` well below the step's timeout (for example, the Temporal model activity's `start_to_close_timeout`). For the same reason, `max_wait=None` doesn't suit durable execution: [`flush()`][pydantic_ai.capabilities.BatchModelRequests.flush] can't be called from workflow code. A [resubmission](#failed-requests) happens inside the step that found the failure, with the same exception.

Other engines record less:

- With the durability capabilities in [Pydantic AI Harness](harness/index.md) for AWS Lambda, Absurd, pgtask and Render Workflows, submitting a request and each check on its batch are durable steps too, but the waits between checks are plain sleeps in the process running the agent. That process has to stay up for as long as the batch takes, within its invocation, claim or task timeout. On AWS Lambda, Absurd and pgtask, a recovered run continues with the same batch, after sleeping again through the waits it already did. A retried Render Workflows entry task, or a run continued from a [Step Persistence](harness/step-persistence.md) snapshot taken while it waited, submits the request in a new batch instead.
- Restate and Airflow record model requests through model wrappers of their own, which batched requests don't go through, so batching isn't recorded there and recovery submits the request again, in a new batch that's billed too.

To wait out long batches on any of these, add [`PendingModelResponse`](#ending-a-run-while-it-waits) to the `output_type` and schedule the next run from the returned message history yourself.

## Errors and resubmission {#failed-requests}

A request that fails in a batch raises the same error, including its category such as [`ModelRateLimitError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRateLimitError] or [`ModelContextWindowExceededError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelContextWindowExceededError], as it would outside one, and fails only its own run.

A request that failed on the provider's side is submitted again in a new batch, as a provider SDK retries a live request. That's a request that expired before the provider got to it, including a Google job that expired, or that's missing from the batch's results, and a request that failed with a rate limit, timeout, conflict, overloaded or other server error. Up to `max_resubmissions` (default 2) new batches are tried, after which the run raises the request's error. A request that failed in a way that would repeat, such as an invalid request, a context window overflow or an exhausted quota, raises its error straight away. So does a request whose batch was cancelled: providers don't cancel batches of their own accord, so a cancelled batch, for example from the provider's console, means someone wanted its work stopped. With `max_resubmissions=0`, every error is raised.

A batch the provider refuses to create, for example because too many requests are already waiting in the project's batches, fails all of its requests with the provider's error, which isn't resubmitted: wait for earlier batches to end, or submit fewer requests at a time.

A check on a batch that fails the way a live request is retried on, for example with a dropped connection or a server error, says nothing about the batch, so the request keeps waiting and the batch is checked again at the next poll. After 3 failed checks in a row, the next failure raises the error.

The number of resubmissions and of failed checks is recorded in the message history, so a run resumed from a history whose batch has failed submits the request again, rather than reading the same failed result every time it's resumed. A resubmitted request waits for its new batch as usual, or, with [`PendingModelResponse`](#ending-a-run-while-it-waits), ends the run with a new `PendingModelResponse`.

## Direct batch requests

[`model_request_batch`][pydantic_ai.direct.model_request_batch] sends a list of [`BatchRequest`][pydantic_ai.models.batch.BatchRequest]s through a model's batch API and waits for all of them. Every request can have its own messages, settings and [request parameters][pydantic_ai.models.ModelRequestParameters], such as tools and output schema. It returns, in request order, each request's response or the [`ModelAPIError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelAPIError] it failed with:

```python {title="batch_direct.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
from pydantic_ai import ModelRequest
from pydantic_ai.direct import model_request_batch
from pydantic_ai.models.batch import BatchRequest

INSTRUCTIONS = 'Classify the sentiment of this product review as positive, negative or mixed. Answer with one word.'
reviews = {
    'review-1': 'Arrived quickly and works perfectly.',
    'review-2': 'Broke after two days, and support never replied.',
}


async def main():
    responses = await model_request_batch(
        '{{ anthropic:medium }}',
        [
            BatchRequest(
                custom_id=review_id,
                messages=[ModelRequest.user_text_prompt(review, instructions=INSTRUCTIONS)],
                model_settings={'max_tokens': 10},
            )
            for review_id, review in reviews.items()
        ],
    )
    for review_id, response in zip(reviews, responses):
        if isinstance(response, Exception):
            print(f'{review_id} failed: {response}')
        else:
            print(f'{review_id}: {response.text}')
            #> review-1: positive
            #> review-2: negative
```

Requests are split into as many batches as the provider requires, by count and size. Unlike with `BatchModelRequests`, `max_requests` defaults to `None`, which takes the provider's own limit. `poll_interval` and `max_poll_interval` set how often batches are checked on, as for `BatchModelRequests`. Requests a batch didn't run, or that failed with a transient error, are [submitted again](#failed-requests) in new batches, up to `max_resubmissions` times, and the call returns once every request has a response or an error that resubmitting wouldn't fix.

A request's own error is returned in its place, but an error creating a batch, checking on one or downloading its results isn't a request's error: the call raises it, after cancelling the batches it created that haven't ended. A check that fails the way a live request is retried on is first tried again at the next poll, as with `BatchModelRequests`. Cancelling the call cancels the batches that haven't ended too.

A request's `request_timeout` setting raises a [`UserError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError], since one request in a batch can't be timed out separately: to limit how long the call waits, cancel it, for example with `asyncio.timeout`. Unlike [`model_request`][pydantic_ai.direct.model_request], `model_request_batch` and the `batch_*` methods below aren't [traced](#tracing).

### The low-level `Model` API {#submit-now-collect-later}

To manage batch jobs yourself, use the `batch_*` methods of [`Model`][pydantic_ai.models.Model] directly. [`batch_encode`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_encode] turns a `BatchRequest` into the provider's format, and [`batch_create`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_create] submits encoded requests and returns a [`Batch`][pydantic_ai.models.batch.Batch] handle. The handle holds only plain data, so you can store it, together with your requests' messages, settings and parameters, which are needed to read the results:

```python {title="batch_submit_collect.py" gateway_toggle="skip"}
import asyncio

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

from pydantic_ai import ModelRequest
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import ModelAPIError
from pydantic_ai.models import infer_model
from pydantic_ai.models.batch import Batch, BatchRequest

INSTRUCTIONS = 'Classify the sentiment of this product review as positive, negative or mixed. Answer with one word.'
reviews = {
    'review-1': 'Arrived quickly and works perfectly.',
    'review-2': 'Broke after two days, and support never replied.',
}
batch_adapter = TypeAdapter(Batch)
model = infer_model('{{ anthropic:medium }}')
requests = [
    BatchRequest(custom_id=review_id, messages=[ModelRequest.user_text_prompt(review, instructions=INSTRUCTIONS)])
    for review_id, review in reviews.items()
]


async def submit() -> bytes:
    batch = await model.batch_create([await model.batch_encode(request) for request in requests])  # (1)!
    return batch_adapter.dump_json(batch)  # (2)!


async def collect(stored_batch: bytes) -> bool:
    batch = await model.batch_status(batch_adapter.validate_json(stored_batch))  # (3)!
    if batch.status != 'ended':
        return False
    requests_by_id = {request.custom_id: request for request in requests}
    for result in await model.batch_results(batch):
        try:
            text = model.batch_decode(result, requests_by_id[result.custom_id]).text
        except ModelAPIError as error:  # (4)!
            text = f'failed: {error}'
        print(f'{result.custom_id}: {text}')
        #> review-1: positive
        #> review-2: negative
    return True


async def main():
    stored = await submit()
    while not await collect(stored):  # (5)!
        await asyncio.sleep(600)
```

1. The requests passed to one `batch_create` call must share a [`group`][pydantic_ai.models.batch.EncodedBatchRequest.group] and fit in one batch, within [`batch_max_requests`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_max_requests] and [`batch_max_bytes`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_max_bytes]; otherwise it raises a `UserError`. `model_request_batch` does that grouping and splitting for you.
2. Store this, for example in a database, and load it wherever you collect the results.
3. Returns the batch's current state, which is the handle to pass to `batch_results` once it has ended.
4. `batch_decode` raises the [`ModelAPIError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelAPIError] the request failed with, if it did. Resubmitting failed requests is up to you, as is handling a request the batch ended without a result for.
5. Or check from a scheduled job.

[`batch_cancel`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_cancel] asks the provider to cancel a batch. `batch_create` doesn't retry a failed submission, because the provider may have created the batch before the connection failed: check the provider's batches before submitting the requests again.

## Details

### Which requests share a batch

Each model request is batched with the model that serves it, however that model was chosen: the agent's model, one passed to the run as `model=`, one a capability's `get_model` such as [`SelectModel`](capabilities/select-model.md) selects, or one a `before_model_request` hook swaps in, whatever the order of the capabilities. A run that switches models partway through puts each request in a batch for the model serving it, and a switch to a model without a [batch API](#supported-models) raises a [`UserError`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError] at that request. A [`FallbackModel`][pydantic_ai.models.fallback.FallbackModel] has no batch API of its own, so batching one raises a `UserError` too.

Requests go into separate batches when the provider can't take them in one: when they use different credentials or endpoints, with OpenAI and Google when they use different models, and with Anthropic when they need different beta flags. Anthropic batches can mix models and settings otherwise. A batch is also split when it would exceed the provider's size limit, [`Model.batch_max_bytes`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_max_bytes], and the provider's limit on requests per batch, [`Model.batch_max_requests`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.batch_max_requests], caps `max_requests`; each provider's page lists its limits. A request too large for any batch raises a `UserError` when it's made.

Since a batch is submitted, checked and collected with one credential, batching refuses clients whose credential can vary or that it can't see: an OpenAI client with an API key callback or a workload identity, an HTTP client with an `auth` of its own, and per-request `extra_headers`. Configure the credential on the provider's client instead. Other settings that only apply to a single live request, such as a per-request `timeout` or `max_retries`, raise a `UserError` too; configure them on the provider's client. See each provider's page for its other limitations.

OpenAI stores batched responses by default, as it does other responses, so `openai_previous_response_id` works across batches; set `openai_store=False` to opt out.

### Request timeouts

A [`request_timeout`][pydantic_ai.settings.ModelSettings.request_timeout] in the model settings covers the whole wait, from when the request is queued until its result arrives. When it passes, the run raises [`ModelRequestTimeout`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRequestTimeout] and the request is withdrawn, which cancels its batch if no other request is waiting on it.

### Streaming and event loops

A batch result arrives all at once, so a streamed run, like one with [`run_stream()`][pydantic_ai.agent.AbstractAgent.run_stream] or [`run_stream_events()`][pydantic_ai.agent.AbstractAgent.run_stream_events], an [`event_stream_handler`](agent.md#streaming-all-events) or a [UI adapter](ui/overview.md), waits for its batch as any run does and then gets each part of the response in one event.

Batching needs an `asyncio` event loop, so it doesn't run under Trio. One `BatchModelRequests` instance can serve runs on several event loops, for example in several threads: each loop's requests go into batches of their own.

### Model wrappers and hooks

`BatchModelRequests` sends requests through the model's batch API methods rather than its `request()`. So a model wrapper inside it, from a capability listed after it, never has `request()` called. A wrapper outside it, from a capability listed before it, has `request()` called for the submission and again for every check of the batch, receiving a response with `state='suspended'` until the result arrives. Put behavior that should run once per model request, like counting or metering requests, in a [`wrap_model_request`](capabilities/custom.md#model-request-hooks) hook instead: model request hooks run once per request, wherever the capability is listed.

### Cancellation and `async with`

Cancelling a run that's waiting abandons its request: Pydantic AI cancels the provider batch once every request it submitted in that batch has been abandoned, and requests the provider already completed may still be billed. A batch submitted by another process, or by another `BatchModelRequests` instance, is left running, since a message history can't be trusted to say which other requests share the batch.

A request a run left for a later run, by ending with a [`PendingModelResponse`](#ending-a-run-while-it-waits), keeps its batch running too. A later run that resumes it and is then cancelled leaves the batch running, since the same history may be resumed again elsewhere. A pending response that an [`after_model_request`](hooks.md#model-request-hooks) hook rejects, by raising or by returning another response, isn't left for a later run: its request is abandoned like a cancelled run's.

Requests waiting on the same submission or check share one task. Using the capability as an async context manager, `async with batching:`, cancels those tasks when it exits, and requests still queued or waiting on them fail with a `UserError`. A request waiting between two checks of its batch isn't affected: its next check runs as usual.

### Tracing

With [instrumentation](logfire.md) enabled, a batch is traced once, in a trace of its own, rather than under whichever run's request happened to start it. Its submission is a `batch <model>` span that links to the `chat` span of every request in the batch, and each check is a `batch check <model>` span within that trace, holding the provider's HTTP requests. Each request's span records the batch's ID as `pydantic_ai.batch.id` and links to the `batch` span, including in a later run that resumes waiting from the message history. That's the `chat` span, or under Temporal, the model activity's span within it.

### Retention

Providers only keep a batch's results for a limited time. OpenAI [deletes a batch's output file](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) 30 days after the batch completes. Anthropic makes [results available](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) for 29 days after the batch was created, counted from its creation rather than from when it ended; the batch itself can still be checked after that. Google [stores results](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api) for 6 weeks by default.

A run resumed from a history whose batch the provider no longer has raises [`SuspendedResponseExpired`][pydantic_ai.exceptions.SuspendedResponseExpired], as a resumed [OpenAI background response](models/openai.md#background-mode) does. The request isn't submitted again, since the provider may have run and billed it: to run it again, resume from the history without the pending response at its end. A key from another project or workspace also gets this error, since the provider won't show it the batch.
