title: Memory
description: "Give a Pydantic AI agent long-term memory across runs: a Markdown notebook it writes and searches, per-user namespaces, and file, SQLite, or Postgres stores."
---

# Memory

Give an agent a persistent notebook that it can update, search, and reuse across runs without loading every stored file into every prompt.

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](index.md#version-policy).

## Notebook model

Memory gives each agent a notebook made of Markdown files:

- `MEMORY.md` is the main notebook. By default, a bounded excerpt and the names of other files are recorded with the user's prompt as delimited user-role context, once per run in which they changed.
- Other files hold longer or focused notes. The model reads them on demand or finds them with bounded text search.

The model gets four tools:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `write_memory` | Append to a file or replace one unique text fragment. Writes use optimistic concurrency and an idempotency identifier derived from the run, its step, and the tool call. |
| `read_memory` | Read a bounded prefix of one memory file. Left out when `FileSystem` can read the files ([Reading memory with `FileSystem`](#reading-memory-with-filesystem)). |
| `delete_memory` | Delete a file. The main notebook is protected. |
| `search_memory` | Search across notebook files, subject to configured result, character, and file-scan limits. |

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import LocalWorkspace
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:large }}',
    capabilities=[LocalWorkspace('.'), Memory(FileStore('.agent-memory'))],
    defer_model_check=True,
)
```

`FileStore` keeps the notes as Markdown files in the run's [workspace](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/), so the model can also open them with its file tools. A run without a workspace fails at its start. With a read-only run workspace, the write and delete tools are hidden; a store with its own workspace follows that workspace's permissions instead. Workspace refusals during mutations become tool failures. To keep them on your machine while the agent works in a sandbox, pass a backend: `FileStore('.', workspace=LocalWorkspaceBackend('/var/lib/myapp/memory'))`.

The namespace is resolved by application code, not supplied to the tools. The model therefore cannot select another user's namespace in a tool call.

### Reading memory with `FileSystem`

When the store is a `FileStore` that keeps its files in the run's workspace (no `workspace=` of its own, and a relative `directory` inside the working directory) and `FileSystem` is on the agent, `read_memory` steps aside for `FileSystem`'s `read_file`. The tool is marked with [`unless_tool_kind`][pydantic_ai.tools.ToolDefinition.unless_tool_kind] set to `READ_FILE_KIND`, so it is left out of every run step that has a tool of that kind. Keep `FileSystem` under its own names for now: a renamed `FileSystem` tool can't be called yet ([#10927](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/10927)). With a `store_resolver`, the store it returns for the run decides. The guidance in the instructions doesn't name a reader, so it is the same in every run and stays in the cached prefix. An instruction block of its own, named `directory`, says where this scope's files are, for example "Memory files are in `.agent-memory/main/` in the workspace; read them with the file-reading tool.", so the model knows even in a run that records no snapshot. The block is there from the first request, empty while no file reader is on the run, and appended to the history when one joins. Its text counts against `max_tokens` with the guidance and the snapshot: when it doesn't fit, `read_memory` stays and the block says nothing; the injected `<memory>` block says so too, and the notices that pointed at `read_memory` (lines left out of the injected notebook, an `old_text` that was not found) name a `read_file` call on the file's path instead.

`InMemoryStore`, `SqliteMemoryStore`, `PostgresMemoryStore` and a `FileStore` with a `workspace=` of its own keep their files where `FileSystem` cannot see them, so with those `read_memory` stays. With `inject_memory=False`, or when the guidance alone fills `max_tokens` so no snapshot fits, `read_memory` stays too: the injected `<memory>` block is where the model learns the files' directory.

The decision is made from the store, not from `FileSystem`'s access rules. A `FileSystem` whose `denied_patterns` cover the memory directory, or whose `allowed_patterns` leave it out, still replaces `read_memory` but cannot open the files. Give the store a `workspace=` of its own to keep `read_memory` in that setup.

The directory includes the namespace. With file tools over the run's workspace, the model can read every namespace's files under `directory`, whether or not `read_memory` is offered, so give the store a `workspace=` of its own when namespaces separate users who must not see each other's memory.

## Injection modes and limits

Automatic injection is on by default. The usage guidance goes in the model instructions, and stored memory goes in a `<memory>` block, a user-role part recorded with the user's prompt. The guidance, `MEMORY.md`, and the list of other files share `max_tokens` (default 2,000, estimated at four characters per token); the default guidance alone uses about 200 of them. `max_lines` also caps the `MEMORY.md` lines shown, and `max_memory_size` caps each backend read. The file listing is bounded by the same budget, so the capability never requests an unbounded file or listing. Whatever does not fit is left out, with a note pointing the model to `read_memory` (or `read_file`, where it replaces `read_memory`) or `search_memory`. When the guidance alone fills the budget, nothing is injected and the `memory.inject` span records `memory.outcome='budget_exhausted'`.

When `heading` is set, the same `## {heading}` labels both the trusted guidance and the user-role memory block.

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

memory = Memory(
    FileStore('.agent-memory'),
    max_tokens=2_000,
    max_lines=200,
)
```

The snapshot is added to the conversation's message history, so every later request sends it unchanged and the cached prompt prefix holds. `Memory` adds one on the first request of a run, with the user's prompt, and only when memory changed since the latest snapshot in the history (or there is none yet). A conversation therefore carries one snapshot per run in which memory changed; earlier ones stay where they were sent, and the default guidance tells the model that a later `<memory>` block for the same memory supersedes its earlier ones. When memory is emptied, the new snapshot says so, under the memory's `heading`. An empty snapshot is skipped only in a fresh conversation, whose history is just the current prompt: anything earlier, such as an older snapshot a provider still sends after another provider's compaction or a summary that kept memory's facts, could still show what was deleted. A snapshot before the latest compaction boundary no longer counts, so the next run records the current memory again.

New or changed memory is not added after tool results, where a model could read it as a new message from the user. The one exception is restoring the run's own snapshot when compaction drops it in the middle of a tool loop, described below. Memory that changes during a run, through `write_memory` or an external update, reaches the model with the next user prompt; the model's own writes are already in the conversation as its tool calls. A snapshot is only added before the model has responded in the run, so a run that starts without a prompt from history ending in tool results or a response (resuming after a deferred tool approval, or continuing a provider-suspended response), or a `Memory` loaded mid-run with `defer_loading=True`, adds none, even if a hook retries its first request; if compaction drops the snapshot such a run started with, that same snapshot is enqueued again, even when the history has none yet: memory reaches the model with the next prompt. A run with no prompt and no tool results, such as `agent.run()` on an empty history, gets its snapshot on that request. If an earlier capability's `before_model_request` retries the run's first request, the snapshot follows the retry feedback, still ahead of any response. Every snapshot is enqueued, so UI adapters stream it as an `EnqueuedMessagesEvent`.

Stored memory and the listed file names go into the snapshot as data: the framework's framing tags in them, such as `<system>`, and `<memory>` itself are escaped, so memory can't close its block or read as the application speaking.

Snapshots are part of the conversation history and reach UI clients: UI adapters stream each new one as it is added and include it in the history they send. Keep that in mind when memory holds anything the user of the UI should not see.

Snapshots are recognized by the metadata on their `TextContent`, `{'origin': 'pydantic-ai-harness.memory.v1', 'scope': ..., 'id': ...}` (the hashed scope and the capability's `id`), never by their text. A history that loses that metadata on the way through a UI client, as a Vercel AI round trip does, gets a fresh snapshot on every run, and its earlier snapshots then look like user messages to `SummarizingCompaction`, which keeps them with `keep_user_messages`. Keep the history on the server when that matters. Snapshots saved by earlier releases, which marked them with a plain string, are recognized and kept.

When combining it with compaction, list compaction before `Memory`, so `Memory` sees the history compaction leaves. If compaction drops the snapshot a run started with, `Memory` enqueues that same snapshot again on the same request, without reading the store again. It lands at the end of the request being sent, after its tool results, which is the one place every compaction keeps, native compaction included; on a later run's first request it records the current memory again if needed.

Set `inject_memory=False` to keep memory out of the conversation entirely. The tools remain available, and the model can fetch memory only when it needs it. Snapshots that earlier runs added stay in the history:

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

memory = Memory(FileStore('.agent-memory'), inject_memory=False)
```

With `injection_errors='ignore'` (the default), a store failure skips automatic injection and emits content-safe telemetry. Spans record the backend type and a hash of the resolved scope; successful injection records counts and whether a snapshot was appended (`memory.appended`), and failures record the exception type. They do not record memory content. Set `injection_errors='raise'` when a run must fail rather than proceed without injected memory. Namespace and store resolver failures always propagate. This setting controls automatic injection only. In the tools, a path that resolves outside the store asks the model to retry, and a workspace failure during `write_memory` or `delete_memory` is returned as a failed tool call unless the workspace is unavailable. The failure message names only the memory file, so backend paths and the namespace stay out of the model's context. A write or delete that keeps conflicting with concurrent changes asks the model to retry. Any other store error ends the run.

## Persistence and concurrency

Writes and deletes are compare-and-swap: a mutation based on stale content fails with a conflict instead of overwriting a concurrent edit. A replayed tool call is not applied twice, and reusing its operation identifier with different arguments raises `MemoryOperationConflictError`. Custom stores must make both checks atomic inside `write` and `delete` rather than composing separate read and write calls.

Every `read` call passes a finite `max_chars` and every `list_paths` call a finite `limit`. When the file is longer, a store returns the bounded prefix with `MemoryFile.truncated=True` and the version of the complete file. A custom `SearchableMemoryStore.search` must honor `max_file_chars` as well as the result limits. `read_memory` marks a truncated result. `write_memory` refuses to append to or edit a file larger than `max_memory_size`, because it would build the new content from a partial read; edit or replace that file in the backing store first.

| Store | Persistence and concurrency boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `InMemoryStore()` | Process lifetime; atomic across tasks using that store instance. Receipts for the 1,024 most recent mutations are kept. |
| `FileStore(directory)` | Markdown files in the run's workspace, or in `workspace=`. Versions are content hashes, and receipts for recent mutations are kept beside the files. One writer per directory. |
| `SqliteMemoryStore(database=...)` | Durable single-host storage; compare-and-swap and idempotency are enforced in database transactions. Receipts accumulate in the `memory_operations` table until you delete old rows. |
| `PostgresMemoryStore(pool)` | Durable shared storage; compare-and-swap and idempotency are enforced in database transactions. Receipts accumulate in the `{table}_operations` table until you delete old rows. The caller owns the pool lifecycle. |

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore, SqliteMemoryStore

local_memory = Memory(FileStore('.agent-memory'))
sqlite_memory = Memory(SqliteMemoryStore(database='.agent-memory.db'))
```

`SqliteMemoryStore` can instead use a caller-owned `sqlite3.Connection`. Because operations run off the event loop, create that connection with `check_same_thread=False` and manage its lifecycle in the application. The connection must be dedicated to the store and idle at the start of every operation; a call fails rather than commit or roll back an active caller transaction.

If a memory path resolves outside its store, the tool asks the model to correct the path. A corrupt receipts file produces a warning and starts a fresh operation journal; restore a backup if replay protection for earlier operations matters.

`FileStore` keeps receipts for its 1,024 most recent mutations in `.memory-operations.json` beside the Markdown files, so a replayed tool call is not applied twice; copy it with them. It serializes its own operations but not those of another store or process writing the same directory, so share one `FileStore` instance, or use `SqliteMemoryStore` or `PostgresMemoryStore` for concurrent writers. Editing a Markdown file outside the capability changes its version, so a write based on the old content fails with a conflict. `FileStore` listings and searches skip symlinked directories, including links that point outside the store.

`PostgresMemoryStore` accepts the driver-neutral `PostgresPool` protocol, so the harness does not require a particular PostgreSQL driver. Install and manage the driver in your application, for example:

```bash
pip/uv-add asyncpg
```

```python {typecheck="skip - asyncpg's pooled connections are untyped proxies, see #10853"}
import asyncpg

from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import PostgresMemoryStore


async def build_memory() -> tuple[Memory[None], asyncpg.Pool]:
    pool = await asyncpg.create_pool('postgres://localhost/app')
    memory = Memory(PostgresMemoryStore(pool))
    return memory, pool
```

Call `build_memory` during application startup and close the returned pool during shutdown. The store does not manage it.

## Namespaces

Use a namespace resolver when one `Agent` serves multiple users. It runs once per run from your typed dependencies, and its result is hidden from the model-facing tool schema.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.workspaces import LocalWorkspaceBackend
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore


@dataclass
class AppDeps:
    user_id: str


agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:large }}',
    deps_type=AppDeps,
    capabilities=[
        Memory(
            FileStore('.', workspace=LocalWorkspaceBackend('/var/lib/myapp/memory')),
            namespace=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.user_id,
        )
    ],
    defer_model_check=True,
)
```

Namespace isolation controls which records the capability addresses. It is not an authorization system for a custom or shared backing store. Validate the identity in application dependencies, restrict backend credentials, and ensure custom stores cannot escape the resolved namespace.

A namespace is one or more `/`-separated segments of letters, digits, `_`, `-`, and `.`; a segment of `.` or one containing `..` raises `ValueError` when the run starts. `FileStore` keeps each namespace in a directory, so on a case-insensitive filesystem, the macOS and Windows default, `Alice` and `alice` share files: normalize the case of the identity before returning it. Windows also drops trailing dots from directory names, so there `alice.` and `alice` share files too. Spans record `memory.scope_hash`, an unsalted hash of the namespace and `agent_name`. It keeps the identity out of telemetry, but anyone who can guess an identity can confirm it.

## Write metadata

When the agent is not the only writer, for example when people can also edit what it remembered about them in your product, a store can record who made each write. `InMemoryStore`, `SqliteMemoryStore` and `PostgresMemoryStore` implement `MetadataMemoryStore`: `write_with_metadata` stores a `Mapping[str, str]` with the content, and `read` returns it as `MemoryFile.metadata`. Set `write_metadata` on `Memory` to record metadata with the model's writes, either as a mapping or as a callable that resolves it from the run for each write. Your application supplies it and it never appears in a tool schema, so the model cannot choose its own provenance. The callable runs inside each `write_memory` call, after the check for a replayed call, so unlike `store_resolver` and `namespace` it need not be deterministic under Temporal or Prefect.

The model's files live at `{namespace}/{agent_name}/{file}`, so with the default `agent_name='main'` your UI edits `{user_id}/main/MEMORY.md` to change the notebook the agent reads.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import SqliteMemoryStore


@dataclass
class AppDeps:
    user_id: str


store = SqliteMemoryStore(database='.agent-memory.db')
agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:large }}',
    deps_type=AppDeps,
    capabilities=[
        Memory(
            store,
            namespace=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.user_id,
            write_metadata=lambda ctx: {'updated_by': 'agent', 'user_id': ctx.deps.user_id},
        )
    ],
    defer_model_check=True,
)


async def save_from_editor(user_id: str, content: str, version: str | None) -> None:
    """Save what the user typed in your memory editor, recording that they typed it."""
    await store.write_with_metadata(
        f'{user_id}/main/MEMORY.md',
        content,
        expected_version=version,
        metadata={'updated_by': 'ui', 'user_id': user_id},
    )


async def last_written_by(user_id: str) -> str | None:
    file = await store.read(f'{user_id}/main/MEMORY.md', max_chars=65_536)
    return None if file is None or file.metadata is None else file.metadata.get('updated_by')
```

Metadata describes the write that produced the current version:

- It is written in the same transaction as the content (under the same lock for `InMemoryStore`), and each write replaces it. A write without metadata, including the model's writes when `write_metadata` is unset, records none, so after the agent edits a file the user typed, the file no longer reads `updated_by='ui'`.
- A delete removes it. A replayed tool call returns the original receipt, which carries no metadata, and leaves the stored metadata as it is; `read` the file for the metadata of its current version. Metadata is not part of the operation fingerprint, so a callable that resolves different metadata on a retry is not a conflict.
- The bundled stores accept string keys and values without NUL characters, at most 4,096 characters as JSON, and `Memory` checks a fixed `write_metadata` mapping when it is constructed. An empty mapping is no metadata. It stays out of the model's context, the memory spans, and the memory snapshot a durable engine journals.
- `PostgresMemoryStore` keeps it in a `write_metadata JSONB` column of its table, so the application can query it, for example `WHERE write_metadata->>'updated_by' = 'ui'`. `SqliteMemoryStore` keeps it as JSON text in a `write_metadata` column. Both add the column to an existing table on first use, and rows written before then read as `metadata=None`.

`Memory(write_metadata=...)` raises `UserError` at construction, or when the run starts for a `store_resolver`, if the store does not implement `MetadataMemoryStore`, rather than drop the metadata. `FileStore` does not implement it: a sidecar file could not change in one atomic step with the Markdown, and the model's file tools could edit it.

A store records write metadata when it has a `write_with_metadata` method, so a custom store opts in by implementing the one `MetadataMemoryStore` declares. It must store the metadata in the same atomic step as the content, and the store's `write` must record none, as the bundled stores' `write` does by calling `write_with_metadata` with `metadata=None`. A custom store that implements only `MemoryStore` keeps working as before without metadata. A subclass of a bundled store that overrides `write` keeps working too; with `write_metadata` set, `Memory` calls `write_with_metadata` instead, so override that method as well.

## Multiple memories on one agent

An agent can carry several `Memory` capabilities at once, for example a personal notebook plus a shared org notebook. Four constraints apply:

- Give each instance a distinct `id`. Instances that share the default `id='memory'` are one capability to the agent: unless they share one store instance and the same settings, constructing the agent raises `UserError`.
- Give each instance a distinct `agent_name` or `namespace` when they should keep separate notes. The resolved scope is where an instance stores its files; two instances with the same scope (and store) read and write the same notebook. Snapshots are tracked by scope and `id` together, so each instance records and supersedes only its own snapshots, even when two share a scope.
- All instances define the same tool names, so wrap every instance but one in `prefix_tools` to keep the tool schemas distinct.
- Set a distinct `heading` on each instance so the model sees the blocks as separate sections. `agent_name` is a storage key and never appears in the prompt, so it can't label them.

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.workspaces import LocalWorkspaceBackend
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

store = FileStore('.', workspace=LocalWorkspaceBackend('/var/lib/myapp/memory'))
agent = Agent(
    '{{ anthropic:large }}',
    capabilities=[
        Memory(store, heading='Your notes'),
        Memory(store, agent_name='org', heading='Org notes', id='org_memory').prefix_tools('org'),
    ],
    defer_model_check=True,
)
```

## Search

`search_memory` performs literal text search and always applies three bounds:

- `max_search_results` limits returned matches, default 10.
- `max_search_result_chars` limits the combined scope-relative filename and snippet text, default 4,000 characters.
- `max_search_files` limits how many files a fallback scan may inspect, default 1,000.

The bundled stores implement `SearchableMemoryStore`. A store counts as searchable when it has a `search` method, so a custom store's `search` must take the arguments `SearchableMemoryStore.search` declares. For a custom store that implements only `MemoryStore`, `search_memory` requests at most `max_search_files + 1` paths, scans at most `max_search_files`, and performs bounded reads. Lexical scoring uses only each scope-relative filename and its bounded content; tenant namespaces and agent names never affect relevance. Implement the optional search protocol for an indexed or semantic backend while preserving the same tenant boundary and result limits. Semantic ranking is not built in.

The bundled stores search only the files directly in the run's scope and skip a deeper scope nested under it, such as namespace `acme/main` under namespace `acme`. The fallback scan for a custom store skips them too, but they still count toward the `max_search_files + 1` paths it requests.

Scoring runs on the event loop and yields after each file, so a scan near the limits slows that search without stalling other runs in the process.

Before backend dispatch, queries are limited to 1,000 characters and 32 unique whitespace-separated terms. Repeated case-insensitive terms are collapsed so they cannot inflate scoring or scan work.

## Configuration

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

Memory(
    FileStore('.agent-memory'),
    store_resolver=None,               # optional per-run store resolver
    agent_name='main',                 # storage segment inside the namespace; never shown to the model
    heading='',                        # optional heading on guidance and injected content
    namespace='',                      # string or per-run resolver
    inject_memory=True,                # False keeps memory out of the conversation
    max_tokens=2_000,                  # finite approximate total injection budget
    max_lines=200,                     # additional main-notebook line limit
    max_memory_size=65_536,            # per-file read, search, and write boundary
    max_search_results=10,
    max_search_result_chars=4_000,
    max_search_files=1_000,
    injection_errors='ignore',         # or 'raise'
    guidance=None,                     # None uses the default notebook guidance
    write_metadata=None,               # needs a MetadataMemoryStore; see Write metadata
)
```

## Agent specs

Register `Memory` as a custom capability type when constructing an agent from a Python spec:

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory

agent = Agent.from_spec(
    {
        'model': '{{ anthropic:large }}',
        'capabilities': [
            {'Memory': {'backend': 'file', 'directory': '.agent-memory'}},
        ],
    },
    custom_capability_types=[Memory],
    defer_model_check=True,
)
```

The serializable backends are `memory`, `file`, and `sqlite`. A namespace callable and a live PostgreSQL pool must be configured in Python.

## Durable execution compatibility

| Execution mode | Support |
| --- | --- |
| Normal `Agent.run` calls | Supported with automatic injection or on-demand tools. |
| Temporal and Prefect | Automatic snapshot loading is a journaled capability operation. On replay, the recorded snapshot is reused. `store_resolver` and a callable `namespace` run before that operation, so they must be deterministic and free of backend I/O; a per-tenant resolver that queries a backend is not workflow-safe. |
| DBOS | Automatic snapshot loading and each memory tool call are DBOS steps. A recovered or forked workflow reuses their recorded results instead of reading or writing the store again. |

`Memory` carries the stable default `id='memory'`, so durable recovery works without configuration. The memory backend and workflow state backend remain independent: durable execution does not make an in-memory notebook persistent.

Each model request that uses automatic snapshot loading records one bounded snapshot result in workflow history, so choose `max_memory_size` and `max_tokens` with the engine's history limits in mind.

## Security and provenance

Memory is model-written, untrusted content that can re-enter future prompts. Keeping it in a delimited user-role part lowers its authority relative to model instructions, but this is not a hard prompt-injection boundary. In stored content, the `<` of a `<memory>` or `</memory>` tag, in any case or spacing, is injected as `<`, so stored text cannot end the block early. Use `inject_memory=False` when less-trusted actors can write to the store, and expose memory only through application-controlled retrieval when stronger isolation is required. Do not store secrets unless the backend, retention policy, and access controls are appropriate. Sanitize content before rendering it into another trust domain.

Memory records do not carry source citations. To record who wrote a file, such as the user in your product or the agent, use [write metadata](#write-metadata) with a `MetadataMemoryStore` rather than a header in the note. Metadata records which writer produced the current version; it does not establish that a remembered claim is true, and neither does optimistic concurrency, which prevents lost updates.

## API reference

- [`pydantic_ai_harness.memory` source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/memory/)
- [Pydantic AI capabilities](../capabilities/overview.md)
- [Pydantic AI hooks](../hooks.md)

The public module exports `Memory`, `MemoryToolset`, the bundled stores, the store protocols, mutation and search result models, and conflict exceptions. Import them from `pydantic_ai_harness.memory`.

# Notion

Let an agent search and change content in a Notion workspace. `Notion` gives the agent every tool Notion's hosted MCP server offers, including tools that make changes. The agent acts with the permissions of the Notion user it connects as.

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](index.md#version-policy).

## Install and connect

```bash
pip/uv-add "pydantic-ai-harness[notion]" "pydantic-ai-slim[openai]"
```

Set `NOTION_ACCESS_TOKEN` to a Notion OAuth access token, or pass `auth=` a token. On your own machine, `auth='oauth'` signs you in through the browser instead. See the [provider setup](https://developers.notion.com/guides/mcp/build-mcp-client).

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness.notion import Notion

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', capabilities=[Notion()])
result = agent.run_sync('Summarize the resources I can access')
print(result.output)
```

## Per-user credentials

`auth` decides which Notion account each run uses:

| `auth` | Account used |
| --- | --- |
| Not set, `None`, or `''` | `NOTION_ACCESS_TOKEN`. If that is not set either, creating the agent raises an error. |
| An access token | That token, for every run. |
| `'oauth'` | The account you sign in to through the browser. This only works on your own machine. |
| A function | Called at the start of each run, and can be async. The token it returns is used for that run. If it returns `None` or `''`, that run has no Notion tools. A function never uses `NOTION_ACCESS_TOKEN`, and must not return `'oauth'`. |

A fixed token or `NOTION_ACCESS_TOKEN` suits a script or an agent on your own machine, where every run is the same account.

In an app where each user connects their own Notion account, one agent serves all of them, so the token cannot be fixed when the agent is created. Pass a function that reads the current user's token from the run's deps:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext
from pydantic_ai_harness.notion import Notion


@dataclass
class Deps:
    notion_token: str | None


def notion_token(ctx: RunContext[Deps]) -> str | None:
    return ctx.deps.notion_token


agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', deps_type=Deps, capabilities=[Notion(auth=notion_token)])
```

Each run connects as its own user, so concurrent runs never share an account. `read_only` applies to every user.

Your app gets each user's token, stores it, and refreshes it. For example, a "Connect Notion" button that signs them in with Notion OAuth and saves the access token to their account. Before each run, put it in the deps, or load it in an async `auth` function.

With durable execution such as Temporal, read the credential from the run's deps rather than from a global, since the function may run in another process. The capability's `id` defaults to `notion`, so `defer_loading=True` works without one. To add more than one `Notion` to an agent, give each a distinct `id` and `tool_prefix`; two that share an `id` but differ raise an error.

## Provider settings

Connect with a Notion OAuth access token. Notion integration tokens are a different kind of credential and do not work with the hosted MCP server. Notion decides which pages and tools the user can reach. Some search and connected-source tools need a matching Notion plan and permissions.

## Tool names

`Notion` has no default prefix, unlike most hosted MCP capabilities: the server's tool names already start with the service, as in `notion-search`, so a default prefix would repeat it (`notion_notion-search`). The agent sees the names as they are. Set `tool_prefix` to put a prefix and `_` in front of them, for example `tool_prefix='work'` gives `work_notion-search`.

`read_only` selects tools by what the server marks as read-only, not by name, so the prefix does not change what it keeps. A [toolset wrapper](../toolsets.md) on `capability.get_toolset()`, such as `filtered()`, sees the names the agent sees, prefix included.

## Tool selection and approval

`read_only=True` keeps only the tools the server marks as read-only. If the server does not mark its read tools, the agent gets none and emits an `MCPReadOnlyNoToolsWarning`. The credential is still what controls access.

To filter tools or require approval in your application, wrap the toolset with the existing [toolset wrappers](../toolsets.md). For example, this asks for approval before every tool call:

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.messages import DeferredToolRequests
from pydantic_ai_harness.notion import Notion

capability = Notion()
agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    toolsets=[capability.get_toolset().approval_required()],
    output_type=[str, DeferredToolRequests],
)
```

Handle the approval requests with the [deferred tools workflow](../deferred-tools.md). To cap the size of tool output, add [Tool Output Limits](tool-output-limits.md).

## Connection customization

Use `auth` in almost every case. Pass `client` only when you need control of the connection itself: your own FastMCP client or transport, for example one with a different authentication scheme, a proxy, or MCP handlers. The client then owns the URL and authentication, so passing `client` together with `auth` raises an error. `read_only` still applies. `include_instructions=False` stops the server's instructions from reaching the model.

A `client` is one connection shared by every run; see [Per-user credentials](#per-user-credentials) to connect each user separately. To use two connections, give each a distinct `id` and `tool_prefix`.

[Source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/notion/)

# Ordinal

`Ordinal` connects an agent to [Ordinal](https://www.tryordinal.com)'s hosted MCP server so it can draft, schedule, and analyze social posts in the signed-in user's workspaces.

[Source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/ordinal/)

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](index.md#version-policy).

## Before you start

Ordinal MCP needs the Pro plan or higher, the same as the REST API. You need an Ordinal account with access to at least one workspace. Ordinal MCP takes an OAuth access token; there is no API key to copy.

Ordinal issues these tokens only through OAuth. Your application gets one by running the standard MCP authorization flow: the server names its authorization server and supports dynamic client registration, so any MCP OAuth client library can sign the user in. Store the token it returns and pass it as `auth` or `ORDINAL_ACCESS_TOKEN`.

If you set up the old server at `https://app.tryordinal.com/api/mcp` with a workspace API key, remove it. Do not use the old and new servers together, because their duplicate tool names confuse the agent.

## Installation

```bash
pip/uv-add "pydantic-ai-harness[ordinal]" "pydantic-ai-slim[openai]"
```

The second package installs the OpenAI provider the example uses. For another model, install that provider's extra instead.

## Connect

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Ordinal

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', capabilities=[Ordinal()])
result = agent.run_sync('List my Ordinal workspaces')
print(result.output)
```

Set `ORDINAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` to an Ordinal access token, or pass `auth=` a token. On your own machine, `auth='oauth'` signs you in through the browser instead. To serve several users from one agent, pass a function instead (see [Per-user credentials](#per-user-credentials)). Then start by listing workspaces. Every other Ordinal tool needs a `workspaceSlug` from `ordinal_get_workspace_context`.

## Per-user credentials

`auth` decides which Ordinal account each run uses:

| `auth` | Account used |
| --- | --- |
| Not set, `None`, or `''` | `ORDINAL_ACCESS_TOKEN`. If that is not set either, creating the agent raises an error. |
| An access token | That token, for every run. |
| `'oauth'` | The account you sign in to through the browser. This only works on your own machine. |
| A function | Called at the start of each run, and can be async. The token it returns is used for that run. If it returns `None` or `''`, that run has no Ordinal tools. A function never uses `ORDINAL_ACCESS_TOKEN`, and must not return `'oauth'`. |

A fixed token or `ORDINAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` suits a script or an agent on your own machine, where every run is the same account.

In an app where each user connects their own Ordinal account, one agent serves all of them, so the token cannot be fixed when the agent is created. Pass a function that reads the current user's token from the run's deps:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai_harness import Ordinal


@dataclass
class Deps:
    ordinal_token: str | None


def ordinal_token(ctx: RunContext[Deps]) -> str | None:
    return ctx.deps.ordinal_token


agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', deps_type=Deps, capabilities=[Ordinal(auth=ordinal_token)])
```

Each run connects as its own user, so concurrent runs never share an account.

Your app gets each user's token, stores it, and refreshes it. For example, a "Connect Ordinal" button that runs the OAuth flow from [Before you start](#before-you-start) and saves the token to their account. Before each run, put it in the deps, or load it in an async `auth` function.

With durable execution such as Temporal, read the token from the run's deps rather than from a global, since the function may run in another process. The capability's `id` defaults to `ordinal`, so `defer_loading=True` works without one. To add more than one `Ordinal` to an agent, give each a distinct `id` and `tool_prefix`; two that share an `id` but differ raise an error.

## Tool names

`Ordinal` has no default prefix, unlike most hosted MCP capabilities: the server's tool names already start with the service, as in `ordinal_get_workspace_context`, so a default prefix would repeat it (`ordinal_ordinal_get_workspace_context`). The agent sees the names as they are. Set `tool_prefix` to put a prefix and `_` in front of them, for example `tool_prefix='work'` gives `work_ordinal_get_workspace_context`.

A [toolset wrapper](../toolsets.md) on `capability.get_toolset()`, such as `filtered()`, sees the names the agent sees, prefix included.

## Tool selection and approval

To filter tools or require approval in your application, wrap the toolset with the existing [toolset wrappers](../toolsets.md). For example, this asks for approval before every tool call, which suits tools that publish or schedule posts:

```python

capability = Ordinal()
agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    toolsets=[capability.get_toolset().approval_required()],

```

Handle the approval requests with the [deferred tools workflow](../deferred-tools.md). To cap the size of tool output, add [Tool Output Limits](tool-output-limits.md).

## Connection customization

Use `auth` in almost every case. Pass `client` only when you need control of the connection itself: your own FastMCP client or transport, for example one with a proxy or MCP handlers. The client then owns the URL and authentication, so passing `client` together with `auth` raises an error. `include_instructions=False` stops the server's own instructions from reaching the agent.

A `client` is one connection shared by every run; see [Per-user credentials](#per-user-credentials) to connect each user separately.

## Define the agent in YAML or JSON

Loading a YAML file also needs the `spec` extra:

```bash
pip/uv-add "pydantic-ai-slim[spec]"
```

```yaml

capabilities:
  - Ordinal: {}
```

```python
agent = Agent.from_file('agent.yaml', custom_capability_types=[Ordinal])
```

Pass `custom_capability_types` so the loader can create `Ordinal` from the file.

title: pgtask Durability
description: Let a Pydantic AI agent run pick up where it left off after a crash, using pgtask, a task queue that keeps its state in Postgres.

# pgtask Durability

`PGTaskDurability` lets an agent run survive a crash. It works with [pgtask](https://github.com/Kludex/pgtask),
a task queue that keeps its state in Postgres.

Run the agent inside a pgtask task, and each model request and tool call is saved to Postgres when
it finishes. If the worker crashes, pgtask runs the task again, and the agent gets the saved results
back instead of calling the model or the tool a second time, so you don't pay twice for finished
work.

Outside a pgtask task nothing is saved and the agent runs as usual, except that tool calls still
follow `parallel_execution_mode`, which runs them one at a time by default (see
[Running tools at the same time](#running-tools-at-the-same-time)).

[Source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/pgtask/)

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](index.md#version-policy).

## Installation

```bash
pip/uv-add "pydantic-ai-harness[pgtask]" "pydantic-ai-slim[openai]"
```

pgtask keeps its state in tables in your database. Create them once per database:

```python {test="skip"}
from pgtask import Client

client = await Client.connect('postgresql://localhost/agents')
await client.migrate()
```

## Quick start

Give the agent a `name` and write a pgtask task that runs it. Then add tasks to the queue, and run a
worker to process them:

```python {test="skip"}
from pgtask import Client, Task, TaskRegistry, Worker
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness.pgtask import PGTaskDurability

tasks = TaskRegistry(queue_name='agents')
agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', name='analyst', capabilities=[PGTaskDurability()])


@tasks.task('analyse')
async def analyse(task: Task, payload: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    result = await agent.run(payload['prompt'])
    return {'output': result.output}


# Add a task to the queue.
client = await Client.connect('postgresql://localhost/agents')
await client.enqueue(analyse.request({'prompt': 'Summarize the Q3 report.'}))

# Run tasks, usually in a separate process.
await Worker('postgresql://localhost/agents', tasks).run()
```

## What happens after a crash

pgtask saves each finished piece of work as a *step*: a name and a result. When a worker crashes,
pgtask runs your task function again from the start. Ordinary code in the function runs again, but
when the agent reaches a model request or tool call that already has a saved step, it uses the saved
result and skips the call.

- A tool that raises `ModelRetry` or `ToolFailed`, or a sub-agent run inside a tool that cancels
  itself or times out (`RunCancelled`), has that outcome saved too, so after a crash the model gets
  the same error and the tool doesn't run again.
- A tool that raises any other exception has nothing saved, so it runs again when pgtask retries the
  task.
- An MCP server is only connected when a call needs it. If every call to it already has a saved
  result, the server isn't contacted.

### Step names

Each step is named after the agent's `name` and the toolset's `id`. These are the names you see in
Postgres, and the reason not to rename an agent or toolset while its tasks are still running.

| Step name | What it saves |
|---|---|
| `{name}__model.request` | a model request |
| `{name}__model.request_stream` | a streamed model request |
| `{name}__model.compact_messages` | a request asking the model to shorten the message history |
| `{name}__model.cancel_suspended_response` | cancelling a response the model provider is still working on in the background |
| `{name}__capability__{capability_id}.{operation}` | work added by another capability |
| `{name}__function_toolset__{id}.validate_args` | checking a tool's arguments with its `args_validator` |
| `{name}__function_toolset__{id}.call_tool:{tool}` | a function tool call |
| `{name}__dynamic_toolset__{id}.get_tools` | building the tools of a `DynamicToolset` |
| `{name}__dynamic_toolset__{id}.call_tool:{tool}` | a `DynamicToolset` tool call |
| `{name}__mcp_server__{id}.get_tools` | fetching an MCP server's tool list |
| `{name}__mcp_server__{id}.get_instructions` | fetching an MCP server's instructions |
| `{name}__mcp_server__{id}.call_tool` | an MCP tool call |
| `{name}__event_stream_handler` | one event passed to `event_stream_handler` |

- A run that uses a model other than the agent's default adds the model's id to the end:
  `{name}__model.request.{model_id}`.
- Characters pgtask doesn't allow in step names become `_`. For example, tools added with
  `@agent.tool` are saved under the toolset id `_agent_`.
- When the same step name comes up more than once in a task, such as the same tool called twice or
  `agent.run()` called twice, pgtask numbers them 0, 1, 2, and so on, in the order they happen.
  Finish one `agent.run()` before starting the next in the same task, so the numbers come out the
  same after a crash.

## Rules

- The agent needs a `name`, or pass `name=` to `PGTaskDurability`. Every function, MCP, and dynamic
  toolset needs its own `id`. `Agent(...)` raises a `UserError` if either is missing.
- Don't rename an agent or toolset while tasks that use it are still running. Their steps are saved
  under the old names, so after a crash the renamed calls run again.
- Tool results are saved as JSON, so tools must return values that can be converted to JSON. A
  result that can't be fails the task, and pgtask retries it until `max_attempts` runs out. If a
  saved result no longer matches the type the call returns, the run fails with
  `CheckpointDecodeError` instead of running the tool again.
- A result is saved only after the call finishes. If the worker crashes after a tool has done
  something but before its result is saved, the tool runs again. Write tools and
  `event_stream_handler` so that running them twice does no harm.
- Inside a task, passing function, MCP, or dynamic toolsets to a single run with
  `run(toolsets=...)` raises a `UserError`. Add them to the agent instead. `ExternalToolset` is
  fine.
- Streaming inside a task isn't live: the whole model response is received and saved first, and
  then its events are sent to you.
- Under [`BatchModelRequests`](../batch.md#durable-execution), submitting a request and each check on its batch are
  saved steps, but the waits between checks are plain sleeps: the task has to keep running for as
  long as the batch takes, within its timeout, and a recovered run sleeps again through the waits
  it already did.

## Running tools at the same time

By default the agent runs tool calls one at a time, inside a task or not. To run the tool calls from
one model response at the same time, pass `parallel_execution_mode='parallel_ordered_events'`. Their
events are sent in the order the model asked for the calls, once all of them finish. Plain
`'parallel'` isn't supported, because the step numbers have to come out the same after a crash.

Keep the default if another capability's `before_tool_execute` or `wrap_tool_execute` hook waits on
something before the tool runs. With tools running at the same time, that wait can change which
call of a tool gets which number, so after a crash a call could get another call's saved result.

## Code Mode

With [Code Mode](code-mode.md), each tool call made from `run_code` is saved as its own step. After a
crash the code in `run_code` runs again, but its tool calls return their saved results.

## Tracing

`PGTaskDurability` adds no spans of its own: the usual agent run, model request, and tool spans
cover the work. pgtask carries the OpenTelemetry trace from the code that added the task to the
worker, so the run's spans appear in the same trace as the `enqueue` call.

## Migrating from `pydantic-ai-pgtask`

Import `PGTaskDurability`, `PGTaskParallelExecutionMode`, and `CheckpointDecodeError` from
`pydantic_ai_harness.pgtask` instead of `pydantic_ai_pgtask`. Steps are saved under the same names
and in the same format as [`pydantic-ai-pgtask`](https://github.com/Kludex/pydantic-ai-pgtask) 0.0.3,
so tasks that are running when you switch continue without repeating work. `DurableTaskContext` and
`current_context` were not carried over.

## Relation to Step Persistence

`PGTaskDurability` lets one run continue after a crash. [Step Persistence](step-persistence.md)
records runs so you can resume, fork, or replay them later. You can use both together.

## Further reading

- [Pydantic AI capabilities](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/overview/)
- [pgtask](https://github.com/Kludex/pgtask)

## API reference

::: pydantic_ai_harness.pgtask.PGTaskDurability

---
title: Planning
description: "Give a Pydantic AI agent a todo list it plans and updates itself, with subtasks, dependencies, SQLite, Postgres, or Redis storage, and a cache-safe reminder."
---

# Planning

`Planning` gives the model a structured, self-updating task list through a small toolset -- and surfaces the current plan back to the model every turn without ever invalidating the prompt cache. It can stay in memory for a single run or persist to SQLite/Postgres, break steps into subtasks with dependencies, and emit events from granular changes.

[Source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/planning/)

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](index.md#version-policy).

## The problem

Long agentic runs drift: the model loses track of what it set out to do and what's left. The usual fix -- keep a running plan and re-inject it into the system prompt each turn -- invalidates the prompt cache. The system prompt sits at the front of the request, so every plan edit changes the cached prefix and forces the whole conversation to be re-processed at full token price.

## The solution

The model owns the plan through the `planning` toolset. The current plan is surfaced back as an ephemeral reminder appended to the tail of each request, led by the capability's single cache breakpoint:

- The reminder is added after the durable history is persisted, so it reaches the model but is never written to `message_history`. No reminders accumulate across turns.
- The reminder opens with a `CachePoint`, which providers attach to the content right before it: the last user prompt, or in a tool loop the latest tool result. That content is what the next request starts with, so on Anthropic, Bedrock and OpenAI each request reads the previous one's prefix back from cache, tool results included, and only the reminder is sent uncached. On OpenRouter the breakpoint stops at the previous user message, so the assistant turns and tool results after it stay outside the explicit prefix.

As with all capability cache breakpoints, provider mapping applies: OpenAI models only receive the `CachePoint` when the model profile enables explicit prompt cache breakpoints, OpenRouter attaches it to the previous user message rather than to a tool result, and models without explicit breakpoints (such as Google's) ignore it. With Anthropic automatic caching (`anthropic_cache`), the automatic breakpoint lands on the reminder, which the next request doesn't contain; the `Planning` breakpoint right before it is the one the next request reads back. A request with no content before the reminder (an `instructions`-only first request) gets the reminder without a breakpoint, since there is no prefix to protect.

A capability listed before `Planning` that also appends a tail part each request puts its content between the durable history and the plan reminder. The `Planning` breakpoint then covers that content too, so its cache entry is only read back while that content stays the same. The earlier capability's own breakpoint still marks the durable history.

## Usage

Construct an `Agent` with `Planning()` in its `capabilities`. The tools are registered automatically and static usage guidance is added to the system prompt:

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning

agent = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', capabilities=[Planning()])

result = agent.run_sync('Refactor the auth module and add tests.')
print(result.output)
```

## The tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `write_plan(items)` | Create or replace the full plan (whole-list replacement). |
| `read_plan()` | Read the current plan with step ids and a progress summary. |
| `add_task(content, active_form)` | Append a single `pending` step. |
| `update_task_status(task_id, status)` | Move one step between statuses by id. |
| `update_task_statuses(updates)` | Apply several status changes in one call, validated all-or-nothing. |
| `remove_task(task_id)` | Delete a step by id. |

Each step is a `content` string, an optional present-continuous `active_form` label, and a `status` (`pending`, `in_progress`, `completed`, `cancelled`). The convention -- stated in the guidance and the tools' replies -- is to keep exactly one step `in_progress`.

All six are registered by default. `tools=` narrows that to an allowlist, and the built-in guidance follows it:

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning

planning = Planning(tools=['write_plan'])  # whole-plan replacement only -- one tool, no step ids to track
```

Naming a tool the current mode does not register raises `ValueError`, as does an unknown key in `descriptions`.

### Subtasks and dependencies

Pass `enable_subtasks=True` to add three more tools, the `blocked` status, and a `hierarchical` view in `read_plan`:

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `add_subtask(parent_id, content, active_form)` | Add a child step under a parent. |
| `set_dependency(task_id, depends_on_id)` | Make one step wait for another; the dependent step is auto-`blocked` until its prerequisite is resolved (completed or cancelled). Self-dependencies, cycles, and duplicates are rejected. |
| `get_available_tasks()` | List steps with no incomplete dependencies -- the ones that can start now. |

`parent_id`, `depends_on`, and the `blocked` status are rejected by `write_plan` unless `enable_subtasks` is set: without the subtask tools nothing reconciles a dependency and no view renders the hierarchy, so storing them would be a write the plan does not reflect.

## Persistence

By default the plan is a fresh, isolated in-memory plan per run. Pass a `store` to persist it:

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning
from pydantic_ai_harness.planning import SqlitePlanStore

planning = Planning(store=SqlitePlanStore('plan.db', session='user-123'))
```

Built-in stores are `InMemoryPlanStore`, `SqlitePlanStore`, `PostgresPlanStore` (over a caller-owned asyncpg pool), and `RedisPlanStore` (over a caller-owned `redis.asyncio` client) -- so the harness needs no database driver. Any `PlanStore` implementation works, and `store_resolver` selects one per run. `SqlitePlanStore` keeps its database on the machine running the agent, not in the workspace. It requires a file-backed database; use `InMemoryPlanStore` for ephemeral plans rather than `':memory:'`.

The tail reminder reads the store on every model request, so a store that raises fails the run rather than degrading -- the reminder is not best-effort. That is deliberate: a plan the model can no longer see is not a state to continue running in silently. Retry and fallback policy belongs to the store, not to `Planning`, and `PlanStore` is a protocol precisely so you can wrap one:

```python
class BestEffort:
    """Serve the last known plan when the backing store is unreachable."""

    def __init__(self, inner: PlanStore) -> None:
        self._inner, self._last = inner, []

    async def get_items(self) -> list[PlanItem]:
        try:
            self._last = await self._inner.get_items()
        except ConnectionError:
            pass
        return self._last

    # ... delegate the other five methods to `self._inner`
```

### Planning and executing in separate runs

A shared store is the whole handoff mechanism between two runs. One agent writes the plan, a second one executes it, and the plan is the only state that crosses between them:

```python
store = SqlitePlanStore('plan.db', session='issue-403')

planner = Agent('{{ anthropic:large }}', capabilities=[Planning(store=store)])
executor = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', capabilities=[Planning(store=store)])

await planner.run('Investigate the issue and write a plan. Do not implement anything.')
await executor.run('Implement the plan.')
```

The executor starts with no `message_history`, so it never pays for the planner's investigation. Its first request carries only the new prompt plus the plan reminder, which the capability rebuilds from the store. That is why the two agents can run on different models: a large-context model can do the reading and the reasoning, and a smaller one can execute against the resulting checklist.

The planner's read-only discipline is a property of how you configure that agent (which toolsets it gets, and what its instructions say), not something the capability enforces.

## Events

Subscribe to typed plan events to react to changes made through the `Planning` tools:

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning
from pydantic_ai_harness.planning import PlanCompletedEvent

agent = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', capabilities=[Planning()])

@agent.on_event(PlanCompletedEvent)
async def announce(ctx, event):
    print('done:', event.item.content)
```

The family contains
`PlanCreatedEvent`, `PlanUpdatedEvent`, `PlanStatusChangedEvent`, `PlanCompletedEvent`, and
`PlanDeletedEvent`; each carries the affected `item` and, for updates, `previous_state`.

Run events come from planning tool paths, including `write_plan`. Direct application mutations on a
`PlanStore` have no run context and do not produce run events. `PlanEventEmitter`, `EventCallback`,
and store `event_emitter` parameters remain supported but are deprecated.

## Why whole-plan replacement

Addressing steps by mutable integer index (insert/remove/reorder) is error-prone for both the code and the model. `write_plan` restates the whole plan each call, so there are no indices to track. Granular edits (`add_task`, `update_task_status`, `remove_task`) instead reference the stable `id` shown by `read_plan`.

## Caching guarantee

The plan is never injected into the system prompt or instructions. Static usage guidance goes there (cache-stable); only the mutable plan rides the ephemeral tail reminder, which lives solely in the per-request copy and is never persisted. Set `inject=False` to disable it. Pydantic AI maps `CachePoint` for models whose profiles support prompt caching; on other models it is ignored.

With a durable-execution capability attached, every plan store call is a journaled capability
operation: the plan read used to build that reminder, and each read and write the plan tools make.
Replay reuses the recorded result instead of calling the store again, so recovering a run doesn't
append a step to a persistent store a second time. Under an engine that runs function tools in workflow code,
like DBOS, a plan tool call runs alone, without overlapping other tool calls, and emits its run
events after its last store call. So its recorded store calls keep the same order on replay,
including relative to the steps an `event_stream_handler` runs for those events.
`Planning` carries the stable default `id='planning'`, so durable recovery works without
configuration.
Engines that run tools and capability operations in a separate worker, like Temporal, don't
carry the run's in-memory plan there: each call resolves its store from the run context. Pass a
persistent `store` or a `store_resolver` (such as `SqlitePlanStore` or `PostgresPlanStore`) to keep
the plan across steps.

## Configuration

```python
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning

Planning(
    guidance=None,           # static system-prompt guidance; None = default, '' = omit
    cache_ttl='5m',          # TTL for the cache breakpoint leading the plan reminder ('5m' | '1h')
    store=None,              # None = fresh in-memory plan per run; or a PlanStore to persist
    enable_subtasks=False,   # add subtask/dependency tools and the 'blocked' status
    inject=True,             # surface the current plan as a cache-safe tail reminder
    tools=None,              # None = every tool the mode registers; or an allowlist of names
    descriptions=None,       # optional per-tool description overrides, keyed by tool name
)
```

## Agent spec (YAML/JSON)

`Planning` works with Pydantic AI's [agent spec](../agent-spec.md):

```yaml
# agent.yaml
model: {{ anthropic:medium }}
capabilities:
  - Planning: {}
```

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness import Planning

agent = Agent.from_file('agent.yaml', custom_capability_types=[Planning])
result = agent.run_sync('...')
print(result.output)
```

## Relationship to `pydantic-ai-todo`

`Planning` incorporates the task-list features of [`pydantic-ai-todo`](https://github.com/vstorm-co/pydantic-ai-todo), a community package by [Vstorm](https://vstorm.co/) -- persistent stores, subtasks, dependencies, and events -- which it supersedes. If you are migrating from `pydantic-ai-todo`, the tools are renamed:

| `pydantic-ai-todo` | `Planning` |
|---|---|
| `write_todos` | `write_plan` |
| `read_todos` | `read_plan` |
| `add_todo` | `add_task` |
| `update_todo_status` / `update_todo_statuses` | `update_task_status` / `update_task_statuses` |
| `remove_todo` | `remove_task` |
| `add_subtask`, `set_dependency`, `get_available_tasks` | unchanged |

Two differences to plan for: there is no connection-string convenience (`create_storage(backend=...)` and friends are gone -- you construct your own asyncpg pool or Redis client, which is what keeps the harness driver-free), and `PlanEvent` carries no `timestamp`, so a consumer that ordered or logged by it supplies its own clock.

## Further reading

- [Pydantic AI capabilities](../capabilities/overview.md)
- [Anthropic prompt caching](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- [Code Mode](code-mode.md) -- another prompt-cache-aware harness capability

## API reference

::: pydantic_ai_harness.planning.Planning
